en: The listeners ask: "What indeed is this book? What is propounded herein? Or what fruit is obtained by hearing it? 1.1.1 The name of the book is *Dāsabodha*. This is a dialogue between a teacher and a disciple. Herein is propounded the clear path of devotion (*bhaktimārga*). 1.1.2 Ninefold devotion as well as knowledge are taught. The definition of detachment (*vairāgya*) is stated. The nature of the inner self (*adhyātman*) is described in many ways. It has been fully set forth. 1.1.3

The intention found in this work is that human beings certainly attain the Divine through devotion. 1.1.4 Herein are set forth the certainty of primary devotion, the certainty of pure knowledge, and the certainty of self-abidance. 1.1.5 Herein are stated the certainty of pure instruction, the certainty of liberation through union (sāyojya), and the certainty of the attainment of liberation. 1.1.6.
The certainty regarding the pure nature, the certainty regarding the state of being bodiless, and the certainty regarding being unstained are what have been described here. || 1.1.7 ||
The determination regarding the Principal Deity, the determination regarding the Principal Devotee, and the determination regarding Jīva and Śiva are stated here [in this section]. 1.1.8.
The determination regarding the primary Brahman, the determination regarding various philosophical views, and the determination as to "Who am I? have been stated here [in this section]. 1.1.9.
The primary characteristic of worship, as well as various characteristics of poetic composition and various characteristics of cleverness, are described herein. 1.1.10.
The definition of that which arises from illusion, the definitions of the five elements, and the definition of who the agent is—these have been stated here. 1.1.11.
Various conceptual constructions have been warded off; various doubts have been severed; various anxieties have been transcended, and various questions have been answered. 1.1.12.
Thus it has been examined in many ways; nevertheless, it is not possible to repeat here everything that has been stated within the body of the treatise. (1.1.13)
Nevertheless, the entire Dāsabodha has been elucidated through its divisions into decades; the translation of each respective decade is provided within that particular decade. (1.1.14)
The consensus of various texts—namely the Upaniṣads, Vedānta, and Śruti—is stated here; primarily, the realization of the Self accompanied by the scriptures is what is taught here. (1.1.15)
Since there is a continuity of various consensus opinions, it cannot be said that [this world] is false; nevertheless, this is capable of being experienced through direct perception. 1.1.16.
If they were to speak this falsely out of malice, then all the scriptures, the consensus of various treatises, and the words of the Blessed One—all of this would be destroyed. 1.1.17.
The Śivagītā, Rāmagītā, Gurugītā, Garbhagītā, Uttaragītā, Avadhūtagītā, as well as the Veda and Vedānta. || 1.1.18 ||
The Bhagavadgītā, the Brahmagītā, the Haṃsagītā, the Pāṇḍavagītā, the Gaṇeśagītā, the Yemagītā, the Upaniṣads, and the Bhāgavatam. || 1.1.19 ||

Thus, various texts have been cited here for the sake of corroboration; the words of the Blessed One have been cited for the purpose of determining the truth as it is. Who indeed could be more fallen than one who lacks faith in the words of the Blessed One? For in this [work], there is no statement devoid of the words of the Blessed One. 1.1.21.
He who utters criticism alone, without even having examined the complete work, is a wicked soul; out of malice, he displays a base pride. 1.1.22.
From arrogance arises envy; from envy arises contempt. At first, the transformation of anger becomes powerful and unavoidable. 1.1.23.
Thus, it is directly perceived that [the mind] has perished within, being agitated by desire and anger, and transformed by the sense of egoism. 1.1.24.
How can one who is defiled by lust and anger be called a virtuous person? (The lustful) Rāhu met with death even after consuming the nectar. 1.1.25.
Let this discourse suffice for now; it should be understood according to its specific context. Nevertheless, the abandonment of pride is the very best of all things. 1.1.26
This has been set forth in a summarized manner as the answer to what was previously asked by the listeners: "What is propounded in this treatise? (1.1.27).
Now I shall declare the fruit of hearing [the teachings]: action is swiftly transformed, and the root of doubt is suddenly severed. 1.1.28.
The path is easily traversed, and there is no requirement for arduous means; thus, the essential point of liberation through union is known. 1.1.29.
Ignorance, suffering, and delusion perish; the attainment of knowledge occurs very swiftly here. Such is the declaration of the fruit found in this treatise. 1.1.30.
That which is called the supreme fortune of yogins—namely, dispassion—is accomplished; and wisdom, accompanied by discernment, is understood according to what is appropriate. 1.1.31.
Deluded people of evil character and inauspicious marks are born with auspicious marks; rogues and logicians are born as discerning people who understand the proper timing. 1.1.32.
Lazily disposed people become industrious; sinners experience remorse; even those who revile others take to the path of devotion. (1.1.33)
Those who are bound become seekers of liberation; the ignorant become exceedingly skillful; even those who are not devotees attain liberation through the path of devotion. || 1.1.34 ||
Various defects are destroyed; the fallen become purified; by merely hearing it, a living being shall attain the supreme state. || 1.1.35 ||
The various perils born of the body and the intellect, the various questions born of doubt, and the various anxieties born of worldly existence—all these perish by the mere hearing [of this]. 1.1.36.
Thus is the declaration of its fruit: by hearing it, the downward course [of rebirth] is warded off, and rest and composure of the mind arise. 1.1.37.
Whatever one's disposition may be, such is one's gain; whatever person should practice envy, he shall obtain that very thing. 1.1.38.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the Commencement of the Work," in the *Śrīdāsabodha*, a dialogue between teacher and disciple. 1.

"It is not known, it is not known—'not this, not this' (neti neti)," so says the Śruti. How then could the intellect of a fool like me possibly prevail there? 1.4.2 I do not know how to contemplate the description of the True Guru; therefore, from afar, I offer my salutations. O Guru, lead me to the further shore! 1.4.3 There was the vain hope of offering praise; however, the support of Māyā has perished. Now, O Lord, O True Guru, I bow to You as You truly are. 1.4.4

"I shall praise through the power of *māyā*"; such was the desire of the mind. Nevertheless, *māyā* was ashamed. "What shall I do? [She thought]. 1.4.5 The Supreme Self, the primary reality, is not perceived; therefore, His image is fashioned. In this very way, by means of *māyā*, I describe the greatness of the true Guru. 1.4.6 According to one's own disposition, the Divine is remembered in meditation; likewise (according to one's own disposition), this true Guru is praised with hymns. 1.4.7
Victory, victory to you, O King of True Gurus! O Sustainer of the Universe, Seed of the Universe, Supreme Person, Treasure of Liberation, Friend of the Wretched!

(1.4.8) By your hand that bestows fearlessness, even this insurmountable *māyā* is warded off, just as darkness flees before the light of the sun. (1.4.9) Darkness is indeed dispelled by the sun; yet, once again, the universe is pervaded by darkness, and at the onset of night, darkness returns. (1.4.10)
Likewise, there is no true guru who prevents birth and death or eradicates ignorance from its very root. 1.4.11 Just as iron never becomes gold, so too the servant of the guru never encounters doubt.
1.4.12 And just as when a certain river reaches the Ganges, upon their meeting it becomes the Ganges itself; thereafter, even with effort, it cannot become separate. 1.4.13

Nevertheless, before that confluence, people consider that river to be merely "an ordinary river"; here, however, it is not so. After attaining realization, the disciple becomes the Master himself. 1.4.14 A jewel from the Pāriṣa mountain does not impart its own quality to iron; gold does not transform the iron. It is not so here: the disciple of a true Guru becomes capable of giving instruction to many people. 1.4.15
In this way, the disciple attains the state of a guru; however, gold does not become gold by means of iron. Therefore, the comparison of a true guru to a crucible is not fitting.

1.4.16 I might consider the ocean as a comparison, yet it is exceedingly salty. Therefore, I should consider the Ocean of Milk; however, even that perishes at the end of a kalpa. 1.4.17 I might speak of Mount Meru as a comparison, yet it is inert, hard, and made of stone. A true guru is not like this; rather, he is tender toward the distressed. 1.4.18

I might employ the sky as a comparison, yet the True Guru is even beyond the sky, being devoid of attributes (*nirguṇa*). Therefore, the example of the sky is inferior for the sake of describing the True Guru. 1.4.19 For the sake of fortitude, I might speak of the earth as a comparison, yet even she perishes at the end of a kalpa. Therefore, the example of the earth is insufficient for the sake of fortitude. 1.4.20 Now, if I were to compare him to the sun, how great is the light of the sun? The scriptures describe its limits; the True Guru, however, is limitless. 1.4.21

Therefore, the sun is inferior to Upamā; the true Guru is the great light of knowledge. Now, if one were to conceive of Śeṣa as a comparison, even he is merely a bearer of burdens. 1.4.22 Now, if I were to speak of water for the sake of comparison, even that would dry up with time. The nature of the true Guru is immovable; it does not dry up.

1.4.23 If one were to conceive of nectar as a comparison for the true Guru, even though the gods who drink nectar follow the path of death, the grace of the true Guru bestows actual immortality. 1.4.24
I might address the True Guru as the Wish-fulfilling Tree (Kalpataru), yet this "True Guru" is a concept that transcends all imagination. Who, then, would accept him as a mere Kalpa-tree?
(1.4.25) Since there is not even a thought in the mind, who asks for the Thought-gem (Cintāmaṇi)? One free from desire does not expect the milking of the Cow of Plenty (Kāmadhenu).

(1.4.26) I might speak of the True Guru as being possessed of Fortune (Lakṣmī), but that Fortune is subject to decay; at the door of the True Guru, however, stands the Fortune of Liberation (Mokṣalakṣmī). (1.4.27)
The heavenly world and the prosperity of Indra—all this perishes with time. That which is attained through the grace of a true guru does not fall away even with time.
(1.4.28) Viṣṇu, Śiva, Brahmā, and all others go to destruction; only the state of the true guru is one and indestructible.

(1.4.29) What comparison could I conceive for that [state], since the entire creation is perishable? To use anything composed of the five elements as a comparison for the true guru is futile. (1.4.30)

Therefore, that the true Guru is beyond description—this alone is my description of him. Only those established within themselves know the signs of his inner abiding. (1.4.31) Thus ends the fourth summary. Now, I shall salute the virtuous ones, who are indeed the very foundation of the supreme reality, by whose cause the knowledge of the supreme reality becomes manifest in the world. (1.5.1)

That reality which is most difficult to attain, and the acquisition of which is incomparable, becomes easily accessible through association with the virtuous. (1.5.2) That reality is indeed manifest; yet no one perceives it, nor is it attained even through the exertion of various spiritual practices.
(1.5.3) Therein, those who investigate are deluded, or even those with eyes become blind; though seeing their own reality, they are unable to perceive it. (1.5.4)
That which is not seen even by a lamp, nor obtained even by various kinds of lights, nor comes within the range of vision even with eye-salve;
|| 1.5.5 || even the full moon, endowed with its sixteen digits, does not illuminate that reality; even the sun, a mass of intense rays, does not illuminate that reality.
|| 1.5.6 || By that light of the Sun [of Consciousness], even a thread of wool becomes visible to the eye, as do various subtle particles and minute objects that appear. || 1.5.7 ||
Even a hair with its tip cut off is illuminated by that which illuminates; yet that very light of the sun does not illuminate the object itself.
(1.5.8) Where objections have been exhausted, where efforts have become weary, and where reasonings have withered in their own attempt to reason about the reality.
(1.5.9) Where the power of discernment has reached its end, where the speech of words falters, and where the agility of the mind has become fruitless. (1.5.10)

Even Śeṣa, who possesses a thousand mouths and is skilled in speech, is utterly exhausted in describing the reality; yet he has not described the reality in its entirety. (1.5.11) Has everything been revealed by the Veda? There is nothing that has not been spoken of in the Veda. Even that Veda does not show the reality. (1.5.12) That very reality is known through one's own experience by means of the company of the virtuous. Who is capable of describing the greatness of that company of the virtuous in words? (1.5.13)

The power of this illusion is wonderful, yet even it does not reveal the mark of the ultimate reality. (Of such a reality,) the virtuous show the means of attaining the infinite. 1.5.14 Reality is indescribable; that very reality is the true nature of the virtuous. Therefore, the description of the virtuous is not the function of words.
1.5.15 The virtuous are the locus of bliss; the virtuous are nothing but happiness itself. The virtuous alone are the root of manifold contentment. 1.5.16

The virtuous are the resting place even for liberation; they are the self-sufficiency even of contentment; or rather, those who are the very proclamation of the fruit of devotion—these are the virtuous. 1.5.17 The virtuous are the field of dharma; the virtuous are the worthy vessel for the realization of one's true nature (*svarūpa*); or rather, the virtuous are the pure land of merit, sanctified even by virtue itself. 1.5.18 The virtuous are the temple of meditative absorption (*samādhi*); the virtuous are the treasury of discrimination (*viveka*); or rather, it must be said that the virtuous are the mother’s home of liberation through union (*sāyujya-mukti*). 1.5.19
The virtuous are the determination of truth; the virtuous are the victory of success; the virtuous are the established time for attainment.
1.5.20 These virtuous ones are adorned with the glory of liberation, by whom countless poor beings have been raised to the status of kings.
1.5.21 Even those who are capable and noble, those who are exceedingly heroic in giving, are not able to bestow this wisdom and discernment. 1.5.22
Great universal monarchs have existed and will exist; yet, no one can bestow the liberation of union (*sāyujya-mukti*).
(1.5.23) That gift which does not exist even within the three worlds, that the virtuous provide. How indeed can the greatness of those holy ones be described?

(1.5.24) That which is distinct from the three worlds and which is inaccessible even to the Vedas—that Supreme Brahman alone becomes manifest within the heart through their grace. (These are the holy ones. (1.5.25)
Such is the greatness of the saint; all other comparisons fall short here. By their grace, the Supreme Self becomes manifest as the foremost.
(1.5.26) Thus ends the fifth chapter in the *Śrī Dāsabodha*, in the dialogue between teacher and disciple. 5.
Now I pay homage to those listeners who are devoted, wise, virtuous, noble, dispassionate, yogis, endowed with excellence, and speakers of truth—I bow to those listeners.
Some are oceans of goodness (*sattva*); some are the very foundations of intelligence; some are listeners who have become mines for various jewels of words—I bow to those listeners.

Those who are enjoyers of the nectar of various meanings, who speak even as they listen to the speaker during discourse, who are the cutters of various doubts, and who are men of certainty—I bow to those listeners.
I bow to those listeners whose power of retention is boundless, who are either incarnations of the Lord or the foremost of the gods themselves, seated here.
(1.6.4) Or rather, I bow to those listeners who constitute a circle of the best of sages, established in purity and tranquility, by whom this assembly hall is exceedingly graced.
(1.6.5) I bow to those listeners in whose hearts the essence of the Vedas shines, in whose mouths Sarasvatī sports, and who, when they speak of literature, appear equal to Bṛhaspati. (1.6.6)

I bow to those listeners who, by their purity, are like fires for all people; who, as suns, radiate rays of brilliance; and who, through their state of being knowers, are more expansive than even the universe. (1.6.7) I bow to those listeners who are ever vigilant, who know the three periods of time, who are always free from egoism, and who possess self-knowledge.
(1.6.8) I bow to those listeners by whom nothing remains unseen, and by whom all objects have been perceived with the mind. (1.6.9)
Whatever we say is already known to them. In that regard, what need is there to speak further with an insistence on their omniscience?
|| 1.6.10 Furthermore, these are seekers of excellence; therefore, I speak without hesitation. Why would fortunate men not serve [this teaching]?

|| 1.6.11 Fortunate men always partake of divine foods, yet for the sake of variety, they also partake of ordinary food. In the same way, my words—though they be common (ordinary)—will also be served. || 1.6.12

The Lord is to be worshipped with devotion according to one's own capacity; there is no thought whatsoever that the Lord should not be worshipped on account of a lack of ritual materials. (1.6.13) Likewise, I am but someone weak in speech, while the listeners are the very embodiment of the Supreme Lord. I, though talkative, have set out for their worship.
(1.6.14) I possess neither learning, nor artistry, nor cleverness, nor skill in composition; I have neither devotion, nor knowledge, nor dispassion, nor even sweetness. (1.6.15)

Such is the play of my speech; nevertheless, since the Lord of the World takes account of one’s inner disposition, I speak with confidence and at length. (1.6.16) O listeners, you are the very embodiments of the Blessed One. What kind of proficiency do I possess therein? I am devoid of intellect and of small wit; nevertheless, I abide with you in a state of friendship.
(1.6.17) Even a fool who is the son of a capable man obtains the capability [of his father]. Therefore, I cultivate friendship with you, the virtuous ones. (1.6.18)
Tigers and lions are fearsome; seeing them, people become afraid. Nevertheless, their cubs play fearlessly in front of them.

(1.6.19) In the same way, I, who have been accepted by you virtuous ones, speak before you. Therefore, your minds will surely carry my concern. (1.6.20) If our person speaks improperly, his words are rectified [by the elders]. There is no need for him to say, "Please complete my deficiencies. (1.6.21)
This characteristic of joy exists in the mind by its very nature. Thus, you noble ones are the mothers and fathers of the world.
Having understood my intention, you should act as is appropriate. Now, let the subsequent discourse be attended to—so says the servant of servants.
The sixth chapter, titled "Praise of the Audience," is concluded.

Now I praise the lords of poets, who are masters of the creation of words; or rather, those who, being the very embodiment of the Supreme Lord, have brought down the Veda. 1.7.1 Or perhaps these are the primary abode of Sarasvatī, the life-breath of various arts; or indeed, they are surely the world of manifold words. 1.7.2 Or else, they are the manifestation of the supreme goal of human existence; or rather, they were born solely to describe the majesty, the divine play, and the noble fame of the Lord of the Universe. 1.7.3

Or rather, these are oceans of the jewels of words; or rather, they are a lake from which pearls have been released; or rather, they are mines of various insights. 1.7.4 These works on the supreme self (*adhyātma*) are like mines; or rather, they are wish-fulfilling gems (*cintāmaṇi*) accompanied by speech; or rather, they are the milkings of various cows of plenty (*kāmadhenu*) obtained by the listeners. 1.7.5 Or rather, these are wish-granting trees (*kalpataru*) for the imagination; or rather, these are the primary refuges for liberation. These poets are the manifold expansions of the liberation of union (*sāyujya-mokṣa*). 1.7.6

Or rather, these are the means for attaining the world beyond; or they are the secret path of yogis; or the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) of the wise has become incarnate. (1.7.7) Or they are the mark of the stainless (*nirañjana*), the sign of the attribute-less (*nirguṇa*), the characteristic of Brahman which is distinct from *māyā*; these are the poets.
(1.7.8) Or they are the essence of the Veda; or the rare attainment of the Supreme Lord; or innate awakening itself has become easily accessible in the form of poets. (1.7.9)

Poets are, indeed, the collyrium that grants vision to the seeker of liberation; poets are the mirror-like means for practitioners; poets are the resolute composure of the perfected ones. (1.7.10) Poets are the refuge of one's own dharma; poets are the speakers of the methods for conquering the mind; poets are, for the righteous, both the embodiment of discipline and the creators of discipline. (1.7.11) Poets are the preservation of dispassion; poets are the ornament of the devotee; poets are the manifold protection of one's own dharma. (1.7.12)

Poets are the abiding love of those who love; poets are the very embodiment of meditation for those established in meditation; poets are the great glory of worshippers, which is spread throughout the world.

1.7.13 The poet is the root of various means; the poet is the fruit of various efforts; the accomplishment of diverse tasks occurs solely through the grace of the poet. 1.7.14 First there is the play of the poet’s speech, and then at the time of hearing, aesthetic flavor (rasa) overflows. Through the poet, poetry is made manifest. 1.7.15
In various ways, the capacity of the learned exists, the power of the capable exists, and the skill of the discerning exists.

(1.7.16) A literary composition (*prabandha*) is fashioned by the poet (*kavi*). By the poet, various movements, various seals, and various meters are created. Poets are both the creators of distinctions between prose and verse, and the creators of their non-distinction. Poets are the creators of word-ornaments (*padālaṅkāra*). (1.7.17)

Poets are the ornaments of creation; poets are the very embodiment of the erotic grace of Fortune; these poets are the means for the preservation of manifold pleasures. 1.7.18 Poets are the ornaments of creation; poets are the very embodiment of the erotic grace of Fortune; these poets are the means for the preservation of manifold pleasures.
1.7.19 Poets assume the forms of gods; poets describe the majesty of the seers; poets praise the power of various scriptures. 1.7.20

If the activity of the poet did not exist, then how could the upliftment of the world occur? Therefore, poets are the foundation of the entire creation. 1.7.21 Without the supreme poet, there is no knowledge of the various sciences; it is from the poet alone that omniscience is attained.
1.7.22 In the past, many poets such as Vālmīki and Vyāsa were born; from them alone do all people derive discernment. 1.7.23
In the past there were poetic works; it was precisely from these that scholars attained scholarship. Through that, supreme proficiency was instilled in the learned.
1.7.24 Thus, in the past there were many great poets; they exist now, and they will continue to exist in the future. Homage to them!
1.7.25 Poets are the embodiments of various forms of ingenuity; or rather, poets are Bṛhaspati himself. Even the Śruti desires to speak through their mouths—to them, homage! 1.7.26

Salutations to those who, for the sole purpose of benefiting others, have provided expositions of various philosophical systems and ultimately articulated their complete doctrines. 1.7.27 Or rather, have these clouds of nectar arrived? Or has a flood of the nine aesthetic sentiments (rasas) been set flowing? Or has a lake of manifold joys overflowed? 1.7.28 Or are these perhaps the treasuries of the treasure-house of discernment manifested in human form? For they are filled with various reflections upon the nature of reality. 1.7.29

Alternatively, these so-called lords of poets are portions protected by the Primordial Power (Ādi-Śakti), such that even diverse objects appear diminished therein. Because all people possess past merit (*pūrva-sukṛta*), they have been obtained through the world.
1.7.30 Alternatively, these so-called lords of poets are pleasure-boats, which are blossomed with inexhaustible bliss and have thus become useful to all people in various applications. 1.7.31

Or rather, these so-called lords of poets are the wealth of the Untainted One; or perhaps they are the state of yoga of the Virāṭ Puruṣa; or else, the scriptural promise of the fruits of devotion has borne its fruit.

1.7.32 Or again, what are called the lords of poets are the prowess of the Lord, which is even vaster than the sky; for the composition of a poet’s work is weightier even than the construction of the universe. 1.7.33 Let this reflection stand. The lords of poets are the very pillars of the world. To them, I offer a prostration with eight limbs, full of devotion. 1.7.34
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Praise of Kaveśvara," in the *Śrīdāsabodha*, a dialogue between teacher and disciple. 7.

Now I salute that entire assembly where liberation is easily attained and where the Lord of the Universe Himself resides. (1.8.1) "I do not dwell in Vaikuṇṭha, nor in the hearts of yogis, nor in the sun; O Nārada, I abide wherever My devotees sing.
(1.8.2) Therefore, this assembly is supreme. Wherever the devotees sing with the chanting of My names and shouts of "Victory! Victory!", that is Vaikuṇṭha. (1.8.3)

That assembly where the constant singing of those devoted with love proceeds, where discourse on the Lord proceeds, where the chanting of Hari’s praises proceeds, and where the exposition of the Vedas proceeds; (that is the assembly).

1.8.4 Where there is the recitation of the attributes of the Supreme Lord, where there is a dialogue concerning various philosophical descriptions, where there is the science of the Self (adhyātmavidyā), and where there is the churning of the distinctions between difference and non-difference; (that is the assembly). ||01.8.5

Where various doubts are dispelled, therein arises resolution; by the eloquence of the assembly members, the form of meditation becomes steady in the minds [of those present]—that is the assembly. 1.8.6 Where the assembly members are devoted, affectionate, imaginative, refined, profound, virtuous, charming, connoisseurs of aesthetic flavor (*rasika*), singers, and steadfast—this is the assembly.

1.8.7 Where they are habituated to action, habituated to right conduct, habituated to generosity, habituated to righteousness, pure, meritorious in character, pure-hearted, and compassionate—this is the assembly. 1.8.8

That assembly where there were yogis, free from passion, indifferent, self-controlled, self-restrained, ascetics, dispassionate, desireless, and dwelling in the forest in many ways; (1.9.9) That assembly where there were staff-bearers, those with matted hair, followers of the Nātha tradition, wearers of ritual hand-gestures (*mudrā*), some lifelong celibates, masters of yoga, (1.9.10) That assembly where there were performers of preparatory rites (*puraścaraṇa*), ascetics, dwellers at sacred fords (*tīrtha*), high-minded ones, great yogis, who, though among the people, behaved like ordinary folk; (1.9.11)

That assembly where there are perfected ones (*siddhas*), holy men (*sādhus*), practitioners (*sādhakas*), purifiers of mantras and yantras, those single-mindedly devoted, worshippers, and those who perceive virtues; 1.9.12 That assembly where there are the virtuous (*santaḥ*), good people (*sajjanāḥ*), the learned (*vidvāṃsaḥ*), knowers of the Vedas, knowers of the scriptures (*śastrajñāḥ*), great persons (*mahājanāḥ*), the awakened (*prabuddhāḥ*), the all-knowing (*sarvajñāḥ*), the stainless (*vimalāḥ*), and those who bring about composure (*samādhānakartāraḥ*);

1.9.13 That assembly where there are yogis, the refined (*vyutpannāḥ*), lords of sages (*ṛṣīśvarāḥ*), the clever (*dhūrtāḥ*), logicians (*tārkikāḥ*), lords of poets (*kavīśvarāḥ*), conquerors of the mind (*manojayinaḥ*), lords of ascetics (*munīśvarāḥ*), and the sky-clad (*digambarāḥ*); 1.9.14
(That assembly) where there are those who know Brahman, those who know the Self, those who know reality, those who know the body, practitioners of yoga, knowers of yoga, and the indifferent;
1.9.15 (That assembly) where there are scholars, experts in the Purāṇas, the learned, Vedic scholars, family priests, reciters, and followers of the Yajurveda;

1.9.16 (That assembly) where there are the most virtuous, the best among those learned in the Vedas, performers of sacrifices, maintainers of the sacred fire, physicians, those who practice the five-syllable mantra, and benefactors of others; 1.9.17
That assembly where there are knowers of the past, present, and future; those who are deeply learned, free from pride, and free from expectations;

(that assembly) 1.9.18 where the members possess the virtues of tranquility, forbearance, and compassion; who are pure, of virtuous character, with purified inner selves, devoted to knowledge, and divine persons—(that assembly) 1.9.19.
How indeed can the extraordinary greatness of those leaders of assemblies be described, in whom there exists the discrimination between the eternal and the non-eternal? 1.8.20

Where the means consisting of hearing exists, and likewise where there is an assembly of people who seek the ultimate truth, there people effortlessly find the means for crossing over. 1.8.21 People endowed with supreme qualities, peaceful, and of virtuous character reside in that assembly; therein, the novelty of eternal bliss is found. 1.8.22 In this assembly, those who are vessels of knowledge, vessels of the arts, vessels of special virtues, and vessels of devotion to the Blessed One meet together. 1.8.23

Wherein those who are active, those who have withdrawn from activity, those of the worldly realm, those of the ultimate truth, householders, forest-dwellers, renunciants, the elderly, the young, and all women and men inwardly perform meditation upon Him who is as dark-blue as a Tamāla tree. To such people of the Supreme Lord, my salutations are offered; through union with them, immediate composure arises.
Salutations to that resounding assembly where the glorification of the Blessed One occurs always and at all times.
(1.8.27) In many scriptures, the virtuous have established with certainty that wherever there is the form of the Blessed One, there is the supreme goal.
(1.8.28) In the Kali age, glorification is preeminent; that assembly is excellent wherein it takes place, because through hearing such glorification, various wicked doubts are destroyed. (1.8.29)
Thus ends the eighth section, titled "The Praise of the Assembly."

Now this ultimate truth is praised; it is the self-interest of practitioners. Or rather, even among efficacious means of accomplishment, this yoga is more efficacious. 1.3.1 Although fundamentally easy, it has become difficult for people because its secret, which consists of association with the virtuous, remains unknown.

1.9.2 Various means of accomplishment yield results in the distant future; the realization of the Self yields immediate fruit. Through this, the essence of the Vedas and Shastras is experienced. 1.9.3

It exists everywhere, yet not even so much as an atom is perceived; it is supremely indifferent, yet it is not seen anywhere in any single place. (1.9.4) There are secret paths in space which capable yogins know; those hidden meanings are not understood by others. (1.9.5) This ultimate reality is the essence of all essences—indivisible, imperishable, boundless, and incapable of being stolen even by thieves. (1.9.6)

For him there is no fear of kings, no fear of fire, nor even any fear of wild beasts. (1.9.7) This supreme Brahman is not displaced from its location, nor does it waver; even through time it does not move—it is steadfast.
(1.9.8) Such is this innate treasure, which never changes; even over a vast period of time, it neither increases nor decreases. (1.9.9)
It is neither exhausted nor lost; nevertheless, without the ointment given by the Guru, it does not even come within the range of vision.
(1.9.10) This is the inherent goal even for those yogis who were previously capable. It is said to be the supreme secret, the ultimate truth.
(1.9.11) By those who have sought it, the goal has been attained; for others, though the goal exists, it has become unattainable even through many lifetimes. (1.9.12)
The absolute truth is such that even the report of birth and death no longer remains; indeed, liberation through union (*sāyujya-mokṣa*) is attained nearby.

(1.9.13) Through discernment, *māyā* comes to an end; through inquiry, the knowledge of the essential and the non-essential arises; and the Supreme Brahman becomes manifest within the mind. (1.9.14) Brahman shines forth as undivided; therein the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) is dissolved, and the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) composed of the five elements attains insignificance. (1.9.15)
The falsity of phenomenal proliferation (*prapañca*) is known; it appears as a mere mental construction (*kalpitā māyā*). Through discernment (*viveka*), the pure Self is grasped.
(1.9.16) When the abiding in Brahman becomes firm in the mind, then doubt flees far away from the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*). The worn-out garment of the visible world falls into decay.
(1.9.17) Such is this ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). For him who practices it, there is his own true interest. How many times shall I address this capable one by his capability? (1.9.18)

By the power of the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), even Brahmā and the other gods find rest; and yogis attain identity with the Supreme Brahman. (1.9.19) For those who are perfected, virtuous, and of great majesty, the ultimate reality is their place of rest. For those ignorant beings who are supremely pure by nature (*sāttvika*), the ultimate reality is their final place of rest through the power of association with the good (*satsaṅga*). (1.9.20) The ultimate reality is the fulfillment of birth. The ultimate reality is the deliverer from saṃsāra. The ultimate reality is the guide to the next world for the righteous. (1.9.21)
The ultimate truth (paramārtha) is the support for ascetics and spiritual practitioners; the ultimate truth reveals the further shore of the ocean of worldly existence.
(1.9.22) He who possesses the ultimate truth is a ruler of a kingdom; he who has no ultimate truth is a beggar. O friend, where else could there be a fitness for this ultimate truth?
(1.9.23) If merit has been accumulated through infinite births, then the ultimate truth arises; from that, the experience of the Supreme Self (paramātman) is born. (1.9.24)
He by whom this Supreme Self is fully realized has indeed made his birth fruitful; any other person is born as a sinner for the sake of destroying the lineage.

(1.9.25) Let it be so. The face of that fool who exerts himself merely within the cycle of worldly existence without attaining the Blessed One is not even worth looking upon. (1.9.26) A wise man should practice the ultimate truth; he should make his body fruitful; and through devotion to Hari, he should uplift his ancestors. (1.9.27)
The ninth chapter is complete.
Blessed, blessed is this human body! This unprecedented quality of the body must be observed: whatever desire is directed toward the ultimate reality, that very desire attains fulfillment.
1.10.1 Through the practice of yoga upon this human body, some have attained the path of devotion; others, having become supremely detached from passion, have gone to mountain caves.
1.10.2 Some wander among sacred pilgrimage sites; some perform preparatory rites (*puraścaraṇa*); and some, with unwavering steadfastness, engage in the constant remembrance of the Name. 1.10.3

By some, austerity was practiced; by some of the highest caliber, yoga was mastered; and by others, through the yoga of practice, proficiency in the Vedas and Shastras was attained. (1.10.4) By some, restraint was achieved through forceful effort, and the body was excessively tormented; by others, through the power of devotion, the Divine was directly perceived.
(1.10.5) Some became renowned Mahatmas, some became celebrated devotees, and some became Siddhas who travel through the sky. (1.10.6)
Some, becoming fire, were absorbed into fire; some became one with water; and some, while people were looking on, took on the form of wind and vanished from sight.
(1.10.7) Some assume many forms; some depart from there while people are watching; and some, remaining seated, wander through various places such as the interior of the ocean.
(1.10.8) Some mount predatory beasts; some move inert objects; and some, by the power of their asceticism, restore the dead to life. (1.10.9)

Some diminish fire, some dry up waters, and some suck out the air from the entire world. (1.10.10) Thus, those by whom various supernatural powers (*siddhis*) were attained—those who have mastered their will through forceful discipline and possess firm resolve—have become Siddhas by the hundreds of thousands. (1.10.11) Some possess mastery of the mind, some mastery of speech, some possess minor powers, and some possess all powers; thus Siddhas of various kinds became renowned. (1.10.12)

Some, by way of the royal road in the form of the ninefold devotion (*navavidhā-bhakti*), attained the happiness of the next world and crossed over. Some yogis reached the realm of Brahman (*brahmabhuvana*) by the secret path.
(1.10.13) Some reached Vaikuṇṭha; some dwelt in Satyaloka; some, having become the very nature of Śiva, took up residence on Kailāsa.

(1.10.14) Some were born as Indras in the world of Indra; some reached the world of the ancestors (*pitṛloka*); some were established among the stars; and some were established in the Ocean of Milk. (1.10.15)
They have attained the desired liberation among these four: *salokatā* (residing in the same world), *samīpatā* (proximity), *sarūpatā* (having the same form), and *sāyujyatā* (union).

Thus, infinite perfected ones (*siddhas*), holy ones (*sādhus*), and virtuous people (*sajjanas*) have been engaged in their own welfare. How much can be described of the majesty of that human body, by whose yoga this has come to pass?
By means of this human body, with the assistance of various spiritual practices (*sādhanas*), and primarily through the discernment of the essential from the non-essential, many have been liberated.
Through the practice of this human body, many have attained the highest states; by abandoning the sense of "I," they became happy through their own bliss.
(1.10.19) Having merely obtained a human body, they have reached the upward path; the root of doubt has been severed by them.

(1.10.20) There is a widespread saying everywhere that there is no means for the attainment of the good state within an animal body; therefore, it is only in a human body that the possibility of reaching the next world exists. (1.10.21)

O virtuous ones, great souls, seers, sages, perfected beings, the saintly, those established in meditative absorption, devotees, the liberated, knowers of Brahman, the dispassionate, yogis, ascetics, …1.10.22… knowers of reality, practitioners of yoga, celibates, the sky-clad, renunciants, followers of the six philosophical systems, and forest-dwellers—all these have attained their state within a human body alone.
1.10.23 Therefore, the human body is the most excellent; it is the best among all bodies, for by its assistance the calamity in the form of the torments of Yama is warded off. 1.10.24
This human body is independent; generally, it does not exist as dependent on others. Nevertheless, it should be spent for the benefit of others and preserved in the form of a good reputation.

(1.10.25) Horses, bulls, cows, buffaloes, various animals, women, and female slaves—even after being released out of compassion by someone, they are bound again by another. (1.10.26) But such is not the case with the human body. Whether one has a desire for the body or not, no one is able to bind it. (1.10.27)

If the human body is lame, it is not fit for action; if it is handless, it cannot serve others. (1.10.28) If the human body is blind, it has mostly gone to waste; or if it is deaf, there is no perception through hearing. (1.10.29) If the human body is mute, then one is unable to express doubt; if the human body is incapacitated, diseased, or decrepit, then it becomes useless. (1.10.30)

If a human body is that of a fool, one afflicted by epilepsy, or possessed by a *piśāca*, it is certainly useless. (1.10.31) One who possesses a complete human body, free from such defects, should swiftly follow the path of the supreme truth. (1.10.32) Even while possessing a body with all its limbs, how great a fool is he who forgets the supreme truth and wanders within the snare of *māyā*? (1.10.33)

Having dug up the earth, a house was constructed; and it was firmly conceived as "mine. Nevertheless, he did not realize that it belonged to many. 1.10.34 The mice say, "This is my house"; the lizards say, "This is my house"; and the flies certainly say, "This is my house. 1.10.35 The wood-boring insects say, "This is my house"; the ants say, "This is my house"; and the tiny ants certainly say, "This is my house. 1.10.36
Scorpions say, "My home! Snakes say, "My home! Oil-drinking insects say, "My home!
Bees say, "My home! Potter-beetles (a species of insect) say, "My home! Wood-boring insects say, "My home in the wood!
Cats say, "My home! Dogs say, "My home! And mongooses certainly say, "My home!"

The *paṅgula* insects say, "My home! The bedbugs say, "My home! The blood-sucking ants say, "My home! The mosquitoes say, "My home! The birds say, "My home! The gadflies and flies say, "My home! The *soṭa* insects say, "My home! The centipedes say, "My home!"

The proliferation of these insects is vast; how much of their detail could possibly be described? All of them claim with certainty, "This is my house. (1.10.43) The beasts say, "This is my house"; the female servants say, "This is my house"; the members of the household say, "This is my house.
(1.10.44) The guests say, "This is my house"; the friends say, "This is my house"; the villagers say, "This is my house. (1.10.45)

"The thieves say, 'My house!'; the king's men say, 'My house!'; the fire says, 'I am reducing my house to ashes! (1.10.46) "Everyone says, 'My house! Even this fool says, 'My house! But when, in the end, the burden of this worldly manifestation becomes unbearable, then he abandons that very place. (1.10.47) "All the houses are ruined; the village has become devoid of people; wild beasts dwell in those houses. (1.10.48)

"Insects, ants, anthills, and mice—this is certainly their home. This wretched fool has departed, having abandoned his house. 1.10.49 Such is the condition of houses; one has personally experienced that the sense of "mine" is false. Birth is a dwelling for only two days; it must be concluded somewhere. 1.10.50 One might say, "The body is mine," yet that body was created for the sake of many. Having made their dwellings upon the heads of living beings, lice drink their blood. 1.10.51

Insects devour the roots of the hair; insects appear in the ulcer; worms are born directly within the abdomen. (1.10.52) The teeth become infested with insects; the eyes become infested with insects; the ears become infested with insects; the ears are filled with flies and gnats.
(1.10.53) Insects clinging to the skin drink the blood; leather-insects enter the flesh; winged insects, having bitten suddenly, fly away. (1.10.54)
Bees, gadflies, and gnats bite; centipedes and leeches drink the blood; scorpions, *gonasa* snakes, *sphurda* snakes, and other serpents bite.
(1.10.55) A body protected since birth is suddenly carried off by a tiger, or else it is forcibly devoured by a wolf.
(1.10.56) Mice and cats bite; dogs and horses tear at the flesh; bears and monkeys kill by crushing the vital breaths. (1.10.57)
Camels bite and drag it up; elephants crush it to powder; bulls suddenly gore it with their horns;

1.10.58 thieves hack it to pieces with a *taḍataḍa* sound; and *piśāca* spirits seize and kill it. Let it be; such is the condition of this body. 1.10.59 Thus, this body belongs to many [beings]. The fool thinks, "This is my body," yet it is stated in the *Tāpatrayavivaraṇa* that this is merely food for many living beings. 1.10.60
If the body is indeed joined to the ultimate reality (paramārtha), then its success has been achieved; otherwise, it goes in vain along the path of death through various afflictions. 1.10.61.
Now, do those worldly fools know the happiness of the ultimate reality? The characteristics of those fools will be stated hereafter. 1.10.62.
Thus ends the tenth section of the first decade.

O Gajānana, whose very nature is the *praṇava*, Ekadanta, Trinayana, salutations to you! Look upon your devotees with a compassionate glance. 2.1.1 O Mother of the Vedas, Śrī Śāradā, daughter of Brahmā, compassionate one, embodiment of manifestation, dwell within my heart. 2.1.2 Having bowed at the feet of the true Guru and having performed the remembrance of Raghunātha, I shall describe the characteristics of a fool for the sake of renunciation. 2.1.3

Some are fools, and some are "foolish-scholars. Listeners should skillfully exercise discernment between the characteristics of both. 2.1.4 The description of the characteristics of the foolish-scholar follows in the next section; let the wise listeners hear it with attentiveness. 2.1.5 Now, the investigation is introduced. Although the characteristics are innumerable, listen with single-minded focus to a few among them. 2.1.6 These are the characteristics of worldly people who lack self-knowledge and are merely ignorant. 2.1.7

He who, having been born from two [parents], considers his wife—who is by nature opposed to them—to be his closest friend, is a fool. 2.1.8 He who, having abandoned all members of his clan, lives under the subjection of a woman and speaks only her intentions, is a fool.
2.1.9 He who is attached to another's wife, dwells in his father-in-law’s house, and chooses a girl of low birth, is a fool. 2.1.10

He who behaves with arrogance in the presence of a capable person, considers himself equal to him, and displays authority despite lacking capability—he is a fool. 2.1.11 He who praises himself, and even when ruined in his own country, delights in singing the glories of his ancestors—he is a fool. 2.1.12 He who laughs without cause, does not perceive discernment even when instructed, and harbors enmity toward many—he is a fool. 2.1.13

He who despises his own people, forms friendships with those belonging to others, and speaks ill of them in their absence when they are inferior to him, is a fool. 2.1.14 He who sleeps while many people are awake, and eats at another’s place, is a fool. 2.1.15 He who brings about his own honor and brings about his own dishonor, and whose mind is ensnared by the seven vices, is a fool. 2.1.16

He who abandons effort out of a desire for the assistance of others, and considers indolence to be contentment—he is a fool. (2.1.17) He who speaks of discernment at home but feels ashamed in an assembly, and who fears to speak—he is a fool. (2.1.18) He who behaves with friendship toward the superior, yet becomes agitated by instruction—he is a fool. (2.1.19) He who instructs those who do not listen, displays his own learning before elders, and casts noble persons into distress—he is a fool. (2.1.20)

He who pursues sense-objects impulsively out of shamelessness, he who pursues sense-objects without restraint—he is a fool. (2.1.21) Even when afflicted by disease, he who does not take medicine, he who does not observe a wholesome diet, he who considers himself satisfied when [only] a little has been attained—he is a fool. (2.1.22) He who travels to a foreign land without [proper] company, he who forms attachments without acquaintance, he who acts with arrogance in a great city—he is a fool. (2.1.23)

He who always pursues pride, who does not know how to guard against pride—he is a fool. (2.1.24) He who, when his servant becomes wealthy, accepts that servant’s servitude, and who is always ill-intentioned—he is a fool.
(2.1.25) He who punishes without considering the cause of an offense (or even without an offense at all), and who displays miserliness for the sake of a small matter—he is a fool. (2.1.26)
He who is averse to the duties toward the gods, averse to the duties toward the ancestors, who is talkative without capability, and whose mouth contains improper words—he is a fool.
(2.1.27) He who is prone to anger toward his own household members, yet is compassionate toward outsiders—he is a fool.
(2.1.28) He who associates with base people, who has secret trysts with another's wife, and who eats while walking on the road—he is a fool. (2.1.29)
He who does not recognize a favor, and moreover, who returns harm for a benefactor, whose actions are deficient and whose speech is excessive—he is a fool.
(2.1.30) He who is prone to anger, a bittern, lazy, filthy, crooked in mind, and devoid of fortitude—he is a fool.
(2.1.31) He who possesses neither learning, nor power, nor wealth, nor personal effort, nor capability, nor honor, yet nevertheless carries a hollow pride—he is a fool. (2.1.32)

One who is cowardly, deceitful, a liar, a doer of evil deeds, crooked, shameless, and whose sleep is excessive—he is a fool. ||2.1.33|| One who wears excellent clothing yet sits at a crossroads [merely for the sake of voiding excrement] and is always seen as if naked—he is a fool.
||2.1.34|| One whose teeth, eyes, ears, hands, clothing, and feet are always dirty—he is a fool. ||2.1.35||
He who sets out during inauspicious moments such as *vaidhṛti* or *vinipāta*, or who brings about his own destruction through ill omens, is a fool.
(2.1.36) He who destroys himself through anger or through contempt out of a wicked mind, and whose intellect lacks firmness, is a fool.
(2.1.37) He who causes distress to friends, who does not gladden them even with mere words, and who bows down only to the base, is a fool. (2.1.38)
He who protects himself excessively, yet disregards those who have come for refuge, and places his trust in worldly fortune—he is a fool.
(2.1.39) He who forgets the Lord, considering only his son, wife, and family to be his true refuge—he is a fool.
(2.1.40) He who does not understand that the fruit corresponds exactly to the action—he is a fool. (2.1.41)

The eightfold nature of desire in women was created by the Lord himself; nevertheless, he who marries many women is a fool. (2.1.42) He who, following after a wicked person, behaves beyond all bounds, and he who does not perceive even manifest objects, is a fool. (2.1.43) He who is a traitor to the gods, a traitor to his guru, a traitor to his mother, a traitor to his father, a traitor to the Brahmins, or a traitor to his master, is a fool. (2.1.44)

He who finds happiness through the suffering of others, he for whom joy arises from the distress of others, and he who grieves over what is past—he is a fool. (2.1.45) He who speaks where there is no respect for himself, who gives testimony even when unasked, and who accepts that which is censurable—he is a fool. (2.1.46) He who speaks while destroying his own or another’s dignity, he who proceeds by an improper path, and he who cultivates friendship with evildoers—he is a fool. (2.1.47)

He who does not know how to protect his own standing, who is constantly seeking diversions, and who, when ridiculed by others, becomes angry and ready for a quarrel—he is a fool. 2.1.48 He who makes harsh promises, who speaks pointlessly, and who, when there is a purpose at hand, maintains silence due to weakness of speech—he is a fool. 2.1.49 He who occupies a high seat in an assembly despite lacking wealth and despite lacking learning, and he who places his trust in kinsmen—he is a fool. 2.1.50

He who reveals his own identity to a thief, who asks for objects he has already seen, and who, out of anger, acts to his own detriment—he is a fool. 2.1.51 He who seeks equality with inferior people, who speaks excessively, and who drinks with the left palm—he is a fool.

2.1.52 He who harbors envy toward those who are capable, who feels despondency over things that cannot be attained even before reaching them, and who commits theft within his own home—he is a fool. 2.1.53
He who, abandoning Jagadīśa, places his trust in a mortal man; he who passes his time without human effort—he is a fool.
2.1.54 He who, due to contact with the miseries of worldly existence, slanders the Divine; he who speaks ill of a friend—he is a fool.
2.1.55 He who does not forgive even a slight offense; he who is always harsh in conduct; he who is a betrayer of trust—he is a fool. 2.1.56

He who is driven out by a capable person from his mind, from whom the assembly recoils, and who changes from moment to moment—he is a fool. (2.1.57) He who dismisses old servants and appoints new ones, and whose assembly is devoid of leaders—he is a fool. (2.1.58) He who acquires wealth through unrighteousness, who deviates from dharma and justice, and who alienates well-disposed people—he is a fool. (2.1.59)

He who, though having a wife, constantly goes to the wives of others; he who consumes the leftovers of many—he is a fool. 2.1.60 He who, having placed his own wealth in the hands of another, desires the wealth of yet another; he who carries out transactions with those inferior to himself—he is a fool. 2.1.61 He who tests the character of a guest; he who dwells in a wretched village; he who is perpetually seized by anxiety—he is a fool. 2.1.62
He who goes where two people are engaged in conversation and sits down there, and he who scratches his head with both hands—he is a fool.
2.1.63 He who spits water into a pool, he who scratches one foot with the other, and he who serves a family of low birth—he is a fool.
2.1.64 He who dandles women and children, he who stays in the presence of ghosts, and he who transgresses the bounds of propriety in the care of dogs—he is a fool. 2.1.65

He who quarrels with another’s wife, he who kills an animal, and he who keeps company with fools—he is a fool. 2.1.66 He who stands watching a quarrel, who does not pacify the quarrel of others, who takes pleasure in watching a quarrel, and who tolerates untruth even while knowing the truth—he is a fool. 2.1.67 He who forgets former acquaintance upon the arrival of prosperity, and who displays arrogance toward gods and Brahmins—he is a fool. 2.1.68

He who is humble only until his own task is completed, but does not perform the work of another, is a fool. 2.1.69 He who omits syllables when reading, or adds extra ones, and does not examine the book, is a fool. 2.1.70 He who does not read the book himself, nor gives it to anyone else for reading, but binds it up and bows down to it, is a fool. 2.1.71

Thus are these characteristics of the fool. By hearing them, wisdom becomes firm; therefore, the wise always listen to these with a one-pointed mind. 2.1.72 There are infinite characteristics, yet only a few have been described according to my understanding. These were spoken for the purpose of renunciation; therefore, the listeners ought to forgive me. 2.1.73 The excellent characteristics are to be adopted, and the characteristics of the fool are to be abandoned. The excellent characteristics will be defined in the next chapter. 2.1.74
Thus ends the summary titled "The Characteristics of a Fool.
May the listeners be attentive! Now I shall describe the supreme qualities by which the mark of omniscience arises.
2.2.1 One should not travel without having asked for the way; one should not eat an unfamiliar fruit; one should not hastily accept a fallen object. 2.2.2
There shall be no excessive speech; there shall be no deceit within one's inner circle; there shall be no marriage with an unworthy bride without prior investigation.

2.2.3 There shall be no speech devoid of reflection; there shall be no movement devoid of thought; there shall be no conduct devoid of moral restraint. 2.2.4 Anger should not be displayed without cause for affection; one should not seek the acquaintance of a thief; one should not travel alone on a path at night. 2.2.5

Sincerity toward people must not be abandoned; evil things must not be accepted; the path of merit must never be forsaken. (2.2.6) Censure must not be practiced, nor should hatred be harbored; one must not associate with the wicked; wealth, wives, and the like must not be seized by force.
(2.2.7) A speaker must not be undermined; unity must not be destroyed; the study of knowledge must never be neglected. (2.2.8)
Let there be no quarrel with the talkative; let there be no dispute with the loquacious; let there never be a breach of association with the virtuous within one's inner circle.
(2.2.9) Excessive anger should not be displayed; distress should not be caused to those dear as life; agitation should not be felt toward spiritual instruction.

(2.2.10) Wrath should not be indulged in moment by moment; one’s own human effort should not be spoken of falsely; one’s own prowess should not be vaunted before an action has been performed. (2.2.11)

A word given in promise must not be forgotten; when the occasion arises, the demonstration of one's capability must not be avoided; and others must not be threatened unless one possesses the power to act as their master. (2.2.12) Contentment must not be sought through indolence; malice must not be harbored in the mind; and an undertaking must not be commenced without thorough investigation.
(2.2.13) One should not take delight in pleasure; effort must not be abandoned; and one should not be distressed by constant hardships. (2.2.14)

One should not feel shame in an assembly; one should not chatter with loquacity; one should never make a wager. (2.2.15) One should not engage in excessive anxiety; one should not live in a state of total indifference; one should not look upon another’s wife with an evil intent. (2.2.16) One should not accept assistance from anyone; if it is accepted, it must not be left unpaid; one should not cause pain to others; one should not commit treachery against trust. (2.2.17)

One should not remain without purity; one should not wear soiled clothing; and a person setting out for business should not be asked, "Where are you going? (2.2.18). One should not abandon personal initiative in all one's affairs; one should not rely on dependence upon others; and one's own burden should not be cast upon another. (2.2.19).
No transaction should be conducted without a written document; a debt should not be accepted from an unreliable person; and one should not go before the royal court without a witness. (2.2.20)

One should not make false accusations; one should not show disrespect toward the assembly. Where one's own words are not respected, one should not speak there oneself. (2.2.21) Even if something has been observed, it should not be treated as if unobserved. A person should not be punished without injustice. One should not practice immorality on the grounds that one possesses physical strength. (2.2.22) One should not eat to excess; one should not sleep for too long. One should not dwell for a long time in the presence of a slanderer. (2.2.23)

One should not personally provide testimony for oneself; one’s own reputation should not be extolled by oneself; and one’s own circle should not be made an object of one's own derision. 2.2.24 One should not smoke; intoxicating substances should not be consumed; and friendship should never be formed with those who are loquacious. 2.2.25 One should never remain idle without purpose; one should not become a vessel for base speech; and even the food of one’s father should not be eaten without effort. 2.2.26
One should not utter improper words with one's mouth; one should not mock another; nor should one accept even a deficiency in one’s own lineage as a virtue.
2.2.27 What has been seen once should not be stolen again; one should not act with excessive miserliness; one should not engage in quarrels with friends.
2.2.28 One should not commit the killing of anyone; one should not give false testimony; one should never behave in an untrustworthy manner. 2.2.29

Slander should not be committed; theft should not be committed; adultery should not be committed; nor should one speak ill of anyone in their absence. (2.2.30) In times of adversity, fortitude must not be abandoned; the quality of courage must not be abandoned; an enemy who has sought refuge must not be punished.
(2.2.31) Intoxication should not arise from wealth; shamelessness should not exist regarding devotion to Hari; transgression of the bounds of propriety should not occur among holy persons. (2.2.32)
One should not associate with a fool; one should not cast one's hand into the darkness; one should not forget a thing through lack of attention.

|| 2.2.33 || Bathing should not be abandoned; the twilight worship (*saṃdhyā-vandana*) should not be abandoned; family tradition should not be violated; and improper conduct should not be practiced out of laziness.

|| 2.2.34 || The stories of Hari should not be abandoned; philosophical inquiry should not be obstructed; and the ultimate truth should not be discarded on account of the power of phenomenal appearance (*prapañca*). || 2.2.35 ||

One’s own duty must not be abandoned; a word promised to the Lord must not be violated; and a wrong path must not be followed without reflection. (2.2.36) There should be no cruelty; the taking of life must not be committed; one should not set out on a journey while it is raining; and one should not set out on a journey at an improper time.

(2.2.37) Upon seeing an assembly, one should not become dejected in body; in the course of debate, a response must not be withheld; and even when faced with reproach, one’s fortitude must not be forsaken. (2.2.38)

One must not exist without a guru. A guru should not be of low birth. One should not consider life or prosperity to be eternal. (2.2.39) The path of truth must not be abandoned; the path of untruth must not be followed; and pride regarding the objects of untruth must not be cultivated. (2.2.40) Ill-repute should be renounced; good reputation should be increased. With discernment and firmness, one should take recourse in the path of truth. (2.2.41)

Those who do not accept these supreme qualities are people devoid of auspicious marks; hear now their characteristics in the following verse. (2.2.42) Thus ends the second section of the second decade.

Listen to the characteristics of the ignorant person; these are the inferior marks of a base family. These have been stated for the purpose of renunciation; by hearing of them, renunciation becomes possible. 2.3.1 An ignorant person brings about only the loss of his birth; he is to be known by the following characteristics—listen!
2.3.2 An ignorant person is distressed by rigorous investigation, because he is filled with defects. 2.3.3
Hypocrisy, arrogance, self-conceit, anger, as well as harshness and ignorance—these, O Pārtha, belong to one born to the demonic nature.

Desire, anger, intoxication, envy, greed, hypocrisy, contempt, pride, tyranny, egoism, hatred, despondency, and conceptualization; 2.3.4 hope, possessiveness, thirst, imagination, anxiety, selfhood, longing, mental cultivation, malice, ignorance, seeking, latent impressions, discontent, and greed; 2.3.5 wish, yearning, medical treatment (or remedy), censure, immorality, vulgarity, constant madness, the conceit of being a knower, disdain, calamity, misfortune, misconduct, and evil tendencies. 2.3.6

Rivalry, exertion, agitation, (in conduct) variety, haste, loquacity, constant activity, lack of activity, and extreme distress—this is false knowledge (kuvidyā). 2.3.7 He who is ill-formed yet of noble lineage, incapable yet wicked, poor yet exceedingly miserly—he is a person of false knowledge (kuvidya). 2.3.8 He who is lazy yet a venomous stinger, weak yet quarrelsome, a trivial speaker yet exceedingly deceitful—he is a person of false knowledge (kuvidya). 2.3.9

He who is foolish yet wrathful, deluded yet loquacious, untruthful yet a talkative chatterer—he is a person of base learning. (2.3.10) He who does not know by himself, yet listens to another; he who, though unlearned, does not study; he who, though not a performer of rites, looks upon action with the mindset of a student—he is a person of base learning. (2.3.11) He who, though ignorant, is distrustful; who, though himself at fault, seeks to deceive others; who, though lacking devotion, hates those who are devoted—he is a person of base learning. (2.3.12)

He who is sinful and censorious, who inflicts harm upon others even when he has fallen into distress, and who, though himself suffering, remains a perpetrator of violence—he is a person of evil learning. (2.3.13) He who, being base, acts as an actor; who, being diseased, performs wicked deeds; who, being wretched, delights in unrighteous tendencies—he is a person of evil learning.

(2.3.14) He who, though physically impaired, is most arrogant; who, though lacking authority, is a skeptic; who is himself devoid of restraint, yet a teacher of discernment to others despite being unfortunate—he is a person of evil learning. (2.3.15)

He who, though lowly, acts like one mad; though inactive, acts with ostentation; though timid, boasts of his own prowess—he is a man of false learning. 2.3.16 He who, though junior, is most arrogant; though deprived of sense-objects, has not desisted from them; though himself fallen, is excessively hateful toward others—he is a man of false learning.
2.3.17 He who is conceited yet shameless; seized by anxiety for wealth yet wicked; hypocritical yet utterly unrestrained—he is a man of false learning. 2.3.18

He who is impure and subject to corruption, who is untruthful and unhelpful, and who possesses inauspicious marks and treats all living beings with contempt—he is a person of false learning. (2.3.19) He who is of small intellect yet a debater, who is miserable yet a seeker of others' faults, and who, being insignificant, torments others with harsh words—he is a person of false learning.

(2.3.20) He who speaks harshly, speaks cruelly, speaks deceitfully, speaks ambiguously, speaks painfully, speaks fiercely, and who is cruel, ruthless, and evil-minded—he is a person of false learning. (2.3.21)

He who speaks deficiently, speaks maliciously, speaks impurely, speaks untruthfully, speaks with hatred, speaks falsely, speaks in vain, or speaks reproachfully—he is a person of false knowledge. 2.3.22 He who is deceitful, crooked, harbors hidden intentions, is mean, incompetent, theatrical, irascible, miserly, or excessively censorious—he is a person of false knowledge. 2.3.23 He who is prone to anger, characterized by darkness (*tamas*), lacks discernment, is sinful, causes harm, suffers from epilepsy, or is possessed by spirits—he is a person of false knowledge. 2.3.24

He who commits suicide, the killing of a woman, the killing of a cow, the killing of a Brahmin, the killing of his mother, or the killing of his father; he who is a great sinner, fallen, and of wicked learning—such a person is a man of false knowledge (kuvidya). 2.3.25 He who is base, an unworthy recipient, a fallacious reasoner, a betrayer of friends, a violator of trust, ungrateful, addicted to lust, fit for hell, an assailant, or a chatterer—such a person is a man of false knowledge (kuvidya). 2.3.26

One who is full of doubt, quarrelsome, contentious, prone to rivalry, unrighteous, contrary to the world, given to grief, grasping, slanderous, addicted to vice, a creator of strife, and a source of harassment—such a person is one of false knowledge. (2.3.27) One who is a tormentor, infamous, impure, a destroyer of stability, a chatterer, lecherous, self-interested, lustful, extroverted, non-giving, firm in his faults, and envious—such a person is one of false knowledge. (2.3.28)

He who is deceitful, foolish, cowardly, inconsistent in action, looking for opportunities at the wrong time, fraudulent, ill-nourished, heretical, a thief, or a robber—that person is one of evil learning (kuvidya).

2.3.29 He who is audacious, lacking in steady conduct, lacking in steady deliberation, fickle, vulgar, garrulous, prone to false imputations, arrogant, fallen, and of wicked intellect—that person is one of evil learning (kuvidya). 2.3.30
He who is a thief, a plunderer, a glutton, a deceiver, a hypocrite, an adulterer, a deluder, and a sorcerer—that person is one of false knowledge (kuvidya).

|| 2.3.31 || He who is fearless, shameless, fond of quarreling, devoid of action, nourished in vain, intoxicated with pride, arrogant, undaunted, illiterate, exceedingly wicked, a universal quarreler, and subject to transformation—that person is one of false knowledge (kuvidya). || 2.3.32 ||

He who is undisciplined, untruthful, ill-behaved, blind, lame, afflicted with consumption, handless, deaf, or suffering from asthma, yet remains full of arrogance—that person is one of false learning. (2.3.33) He who is devoid of knowledge, devoid of wealth, devoid of noble lineage, devoid of fortune, devoid of power, devoid of capability, devoid of merit, and lives on alms—that person is one of false learning. (2.3.34)

He who is deficient in strength, deficient in arts, devoid of the seal of tradition, devoid of initiation, deficient in charm, with deficient limbs, or with redundant limbs—that person is one of false knowledge. (2.3.35) He who is devoid of reasoning, devoid of intellect, devoid of right conduct, devoid of inquiry, devoid of action, devoid of courage, devoid of discrimination, and full of doubt—that person is one of false knowledge. (2.3.36) He who is devoid of devotion, devoid of feeling, devoid of wisdom, devoid of dispassion, devoid of peace, devoid of forgiveness, and devoid of everything—mean and base—that person is one of false knowledge. (2.3.37)

That person who is unfortunate—who knows not the proper occasion, knows not the right time, knows not the effort, knows not the practice, knows not uprightness, and knows not friendliness—is a person of false learning. Let it be so; thus, it should be understood by the listeners that a person of false learning is indeed a dwelling place for various distortions and family-defiling traits. That is a person of false learning.
Thus are the characteristics of false knowledge; they should be heard and abandoned. It is not proper to maintain them under the influence of conceit. Such a person is one of false knowledge. 2.3.40.
Thus ends the section titled "The Characteristics of False Knowledge."
The fourth section of the second decade.
The human body is indeed the fruit of various well-performed deeds (*sukṛta*). Even there, if fortune bears fruit, the path of the righteous (*sanmārga*) is attained.

2.4.1 Even within the human body, the Brahmin body is a distinction. Even there, ritual bathing, the twilight prayers (*sandhyāvandana*), virtuous inclinations (*sadvāsanā*), and the worship of the Lord (*bhagavadbhajana*) come about through prior merit.
2.4.2 Supreme is devotion to the Lord, and even therein, association with the virtuous (*satsamāgama*) is supreme. Through these two, time becomes meaningful; this is the highest gain. 2.4.3

At its root is the true state of being, which is love; within that is the assembly of devotees, and within that is the great festival of the narrations of Hari. In this way, love becomes doubled. 2.4.4 Having attained a human body, one must make it meaningful so that the rare world beyond may be obtained.
2.4.5 One should perform the actions prescribed by injunction, or the duty of compassion, or the duty of charity, or the easily accessible worship of the Lord. 2.4.6
Through remorse, one should practice the renunciation of sense objects; or else, one should practice the yoga of devotion (*bhaktiyoga*); or else, one should associate with virtuous people.

2.4.7 Various scriptures should be studied; or else, one should undertake pilgrimages to sacred sites (*tīrthāṭana*); or else, for the sake of destroying sin, one should perform preparatory rites (*puraścaraṇa*).

2.4.8 Or else, one should perform service to others (*paropakāra*); or else, one should engage in the investigation of knowledge (*jñānavicāra*); or else, one should investigate the essence and non-essence of what has been heard and determined. 2.4.9

The command of the Vedas must be observed; the ritual section (karmakāṇḍa) must be performed; meditation (upāsanā) must be practiced. Through this, the qualification for knowledge (jñānādhikāra) is attained.

2.4.10 Having performed worship by whatever means possible—whether with body, speech, mind, leaf, flower, fruit, or water—one must make one’s life meaningful. 2.4.11 One must make one’s birth fruitful. If that is not done, life will be merely a useless burden upon the earth. 2.4.12
In this human body, that alone is appropriate which is the means for achieving one's own welfare. To the best of one’s ability, both the mind and wealth should be applied toward the highest goal.

(2.4.13) He in whose mind there is nothing whatsoever directed toward these [ends] exists in the world as one who is practically dead; by him, having been born, his mother has been made to suffer in vain.

(2.4.14) There is no performance of the twilight prayers (*saṃdhyā-vandana*), no ritual bathing, no devotion, no worship of deities, no sacred formula (*mantra*), no recitation (*japa*), no meditation (*dhyāna*), and no mental worship... (2.4.15)

There is no devotion, no love, no steadfastness, no self-restraint, no deity, no dharma, no honoring of guests, and no welcoming of visitors... 2.4.16 There is no virtuous intellect, no quality, no speaking, no listening, and no investigation into the supreme self... 2.4.17 There is no association with the good, no pure mental disposition, and through the intoxication of falsehood, there is no attainment of liberation. 2.4.18

There is no policy, no justice, no means for merit, and no means for the next world consisting of the investigation of what is proper and improper... 2.4.19 There is no knowledge, no power, no state of cleverness, no art, and no skill in beautiful speech... 2.4.20 There is no peace, no forbearance, no initiation, no friendliness, and no means for accomplishing the auspicious or the inauspicious... 2.4.21

There is no purity, no one’s own duty (*svadharma*), no proper conduct, no discernment, no concern for this world, and no performance of rites for the next world; there exists only action that accords with the whims of the mind.
(2.4.22) There is no ritual action, no worship, no knowledge, no dispassion, no yoga, and no fortitude; nothing at all is seen among these.
(2.4.23) There is no cessation [of worldly activity], no renunciation, no equanimity, no virtuous marks, no reverence toward the Supreme Lord, and no love for the Supreme Lord... (2.4.24)
There is no contentment with the virtues of others, no experience of happiness through helping others, and not even a trace of devotion to Hari within their hearts...
(2.4.25) Those people who are thus, though living, are equal to the dead; one should not engage in conversation with such unholy persons.
(2.4.26) Only for him who possesses the collection of meritorious means does devotion to the Lord arise in the mind; as people act, so do they attain. (2.4.27)
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Exposition of Devotion," in the second decade.
The fifth section of the second chapter.

Fundamentally, the body consists of the three *guṇas*, being composed of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*. Among these, the *sattva* quality is the most excellent. (2.5.1) A living being attains devotion to the Blessed One through the *sattva* quality; through the *rajas* quality, one attains rebirth; and through the *tamas* quality, one attains a downward course. (2.5.2) Those established in *sattva* go upward; those characterized by *rajas* remain in the middle.
Those who abide in the function of the lowest quality (*guṇa*), the *tāmasas*, go downward;

even there, there are two divisions: the pure (*śuddha*) and the variegated (*śabala*). All of that will be explained. That which is free from impurity is the pure; that which is obstructive is the variegated. (2.5.3) O wise ones, listen with skill to the characteristics of the pure and the variegated: that which is conducive to the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) is the pure; that which is conducive to worldly existence (*saṃsāra*) is the variegated. (2.5.4)

Such is the condition of worldly beings that all three *guṇas* exist within the body; when one arrives, the other two depart. (2.5.5) Life proceeds by means of these very qualities—*rajas*, *tamas*, and *sattva*. Among them, I shall now present a description of the *rajas* quality.
(2.5.6) When the *rajas* quality enters the body, attentive and discerning listeners should listen carefully to how a person behaves. (2.5.7)

"He who determines, 'This is my house, this is my worldly expansion; how has the Lord attained greatness here?'—he is characterized by the quality of passion (rajas). 2.5.8 "He who thinks only of these people—the mother, the father, the wife, the son, the daughter-in-law, and the daughter—he is characterized by the quality of passion. 2.5.9 "He for whom it is thought, 'One should eat well, one should drink well, fine clothing should be worn, fine ornaments should be maintained, and another's object should be desired'—he is characterized by the quality of passion. 2.5.10"

"What is dharma? What is charity? What is recitation? What is meditation?"—he who does not thus investigate between sin and merit possesses the quality of passion (rajas). 5.11 He knows not valor, he knows not religious observance; he pays no heed to the guest, nor to the visitor; improper conduct always dwells in his mind—he possesses the quality of passion. 2.5.12 The accumulation of wealth and grain, a mind attached to material objects, and an exceedingly miserly way of life—this is the quality of passion. 2.5.13
"He am young, I am handsome, I am strong, I am clever, I am the best of all"—he who speaks thus possesses the quality of *rajas*.
