2.5.14 "The land is mine, the village is mine, the house is mine, the position is mine"—in whose mind there is such greed, he possesses the quality of *rajas*. 2.5.15 "May everything belonging to another perish; may everything belong to me alone"—in whose contemplation this is, he possesses the quality of *rajas*. 2.5.16
Deceit, envy, contempt, and the transformation of desire—when these arise within one's body, that is the quality of *rajas*.
2.5.17 Affection for a child, love for a wife, and greed for all [people]—that is the quality of *rajas*.
2.5.18 At whatever time affection toward one's kinsmen arises in the mind, at that very moment the arrival of the quality of *rajas* occurs swiftly. 2.5.19

"He constantly broods over the peril, thinking, 'There is much suffering in saṃsāra; how indeed shall I reach the further shore?'—that is the quality of rajas. 2.5.20 Or, whatever was enjoyed in the past is repeatedly recalled by the mind; because of that, only suffering increases—this is the quality of rajas. 2.5.21 Having observed prosperity, a desire for it arises; the mind becomes distressed with longing—this is the quality of rajas. 2.5.22"

Whatever is beheld with the eye, that very thing is craved by the mind; if it is not obtained, then suffering arises—this is the quality of *rajas*. 2.5.23 The mind delights in diversion; it sings of amorous passion; it takes pleasure in colors, stages, and melodies—this is the quality of *rajas*. 2.5.24 Sportiveness, mockery, censure, dispute, constant laughter, and constant diversion—this is the quality of *rajas*. 2.5.25
Excessive laziness, or various forms of entertainment and play, or a preoccupation with sensual enjoyments—this is the quality of *rajas*.
2.5.26 An artist, one who assumes many forms, one skilled in watching dramatic performances, or one who provides wealth for various amusements—this is the quality of *rajas*.
2.5.27 Excessive attachment to intoxicating substances, recollection of vulgar objects of sense, and a delight in the company of the low-born—this is the quality of *rajas*. 2.5.28

The desire for theft, the desire to expose the shortcomings of others, and agitation regarding constant observances—this is the quality of *rajas*. 2.5.29 Shame regarding divine duties, exertion for the sake of the belly, and attachment to worldly proliferation—this is the quality of *rajas*. 2.5.30 Greed for sweet morsels of food, and such regard for nourishing the body that one cannot endure fasting—this is the quality of *rajas*. 2.5.31

That which is characterized by passion (*śṛṅgārika*) is dear; that which is filled with devotion and dispassion (*vairāgya*) is not dear. That the mind is delighted solely in the manifestation of artistic skills (*kalā*) is the quality of *rajas*.

(2.5.32) Ignorance regarding the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), and that which forcibly generates attachment toward all objects, is the quality of *rajas*. (2.5.33) Let this be the quality of *rajas*. Under the influence of greed, it brings about birth and death. It is powerful in the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), and therefore it subjects one to terrible suffering. (2.5.34)

Now, as long as the quality of *rajas* persists, one does not progress; *saṃsāra* does not perish, for latent impressions remain attached to the phenomenal world (*prapañca*). What indeed is the means here?

|| 2.5.35 || There is but one means: devotion to the Blessed Lord (*bhagavad-bhakti*). Even if dispassion (*vairāgya*) is not yet firm, nevertheless, one should perform worship according to one's ability.
|| 2.5.36 || With body, speech, mind, leaf, flower, fruit, or water—offered with a devoted heart—one’s actions should be made meaningful. || 2.5.37 ||

One should acquire the merit of giving according to one's capacity; however, non-duality with the Blessed One must be protected above all. Whether in happiness or in suffering, one should practice only the contemplation of the Divine. (2.5.38) At the beginning and at the end, there is only the Supreme Lord; it is only in the middle that Māyā has descended. Therefore, a state of complete devotion should be directed toward the Blessed One alone.
(2.5.39) Thus, the variegated quality of *rajas* has been described in brief. Now, that which is pure is the ultimate reality. (2.5.40)
Its characteristic resides in the quality of goodness (*sattva-guṇa*). That pure *rajas* is the root of devotion.
2.5.41 Thus has the *rajas*-quality been described; it has been experienced by the listeners with their minds. Hereafter, the *tamas*-quality is to be heard.
2.5.42 Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the *Rajas*-Quality."
The sixth section of the second decade.
Previously, the quality of *rajas*, along with its characteristics and activity, was described. Now I shall describe the quality of *tamas*; listen.
2.6.1 When there is contact with suffering in this worldly existence, weariness arises, or else anger erupts; that is the quality of *tamas*.
2.6.2 When the body is filled with anger, one does not recognize one's mother, nor does one recognize one's father; one strikes one's brother, sister, and wife—that is the quality of *tamas*. 2.6.3
"The destruction of another must be carried out, or else one's own self must be destroyed"—thinking thus, that which causes one to forget one's very self is the quality of darkness (*tamoguṇa*).

2.6.4 The transformation of anger pervades the body; by means of it, one wanders like a *piśāca*. That which cannot be restrained even by various means is the quality of darkness. 2.6.5 The conduct in which there is the falling of a weapon upon oneself as well as the destruction of another is the quality of darkness. 2.6.6

The battle is to be witnessed with the eyes; one goes wherever the battle is—such a place where there is passion is the quality of *tamas*. (2.6.7) Delusion is unbroken; even a certainty formed by it perishes. One who sleeps excessively is characterized by the quality of *tamas*. (2.6.8) He whose hunger is great, who perceives neither sweetness nor bitterness, and whose state is one of stupor—that is the quality of *tamas*. (2.6.9)

If one thinks, "He who was a vessel of affection is dead; therefore, I too must die," and commits suicide—that is the quality of *tamas*. (2.6.10) Delight in killing insects, ants, or wild beasts—that person who is utterly devoid of compassion possesses the quality of *tamas*. (2.6.11) The approval of killing a woman, a child, a Brahmin, or a cow for the sake of wealth—that is the quality of *tamas*. (2.6.12)

The desire to drink poison out of anger, or the longing for the slaughter of another, is the quality of *tamas*. 2.6.13 Holding a deceitful disposition in the mind and causing harm to another, being constantly intoxicated and always arrogant, is the quality of *tamas*. 2.6.14 The wish that "there may be a quarrel," the desire for combat, and the manifestation of hatred in the heart—this is the quality of *tamas*. 2.6.15
War is to be witnessed, war is to be heard, one must personally fight, kill, or die—that is the quality of *tamas*.
(2.6.16) Devotion is to be broken by envy, temples are to be demolished, and fruit-bearing trees are to be cut down—that is the quality of *tamas*.
(2.6.17) Aversion toward virtuous deeds, delight in various faults, and a lack of fear regarding sin in the mind—that is the quality of *tamas*. (2.6.18)
The destruction of the mental state directed toward Brahman, the distressing of living beings, and an excessive inclination toward negligence—this is the quality of *tamas*.

(2.6.19) It brings about destruction by fire, it brings about destruction by weapons, it brings about destruction by possession by spirits, and it brings about destruction by poison; likewise, that which causes the decay of living beings through envy is the quality of *tamas*. (2.6.20) Contentment derived from the suffering of others, delight in cruelty, and a lack of revulsion toward the objects of worldly existence—this is the quality of *tamas*. (2.6.21)

A quarrel must be provoked, and one must personally witness the spectacle; such a base inclination arises—that is the quality of darkness (tamas). ||2.6.22|| If wealth is acquired, it must cause suffering to living beings; there is no compassion in the heart—that is the quality of darkness.

||2.6.23|| Devotion is not pleasing, spiritual sentiment is not pleasing, a sacred pilgrimage site is not pleasing, nor is a deity pleasing; the Vedas, scriptures, and so forth are not desired—that is the quality of darkness. ||2.6.24||

There is no fixed rule regarding bathing or the twilight prayers (*sandhyā-vandana*). He who falls away from his own duty (*svadharma*), performs what ought not to be done, and is characterized by the quality of darkness (*tamoguṇa*)—[he is so defined]. (2.6.25) He who does not heed the words of his elder brother, father, or mother, and departs in a sudden fit of anger, is characterized by the quality of darkness (*tamoguṇa*). (2.6.26) Eating without performing one's duties, sitting without performing one's duties, living without performing one's duties, and having no remembrance [of sacred things]—that is the quality of darkness (*tamoguṇa*). (2.6.27)
The practice of black magic (*abhicāra-vidyā*), the desire for the science of weapons, and the desire for the science of wrestling—this is the quality of darkness (*tamaḥ*).

(2.6.28) To inflict bodily suffering by means of a hook or a chain, or to have one's tongue cut off by a wooden machine, and so forth—whatever one does out of a desire for worldly gain in this life, that is the quality of darkness.
(2.6.29) Holding fire upon one's own head, burning one's own limbs with a lamp, or piercing one's own body with a weapon—this is the quality of darkness. (2.6.30)
Offering one's head to the deity, or offering a limb of the body, or casting the body down from a high place—this is the quality of *tamas*.

(2.6.31) Self-restraint in the presence of the deity, prostrating one's own body before the deity, or committing suicide at the deity’s gateway—this is the quality of *tamas*. (2.6.32) Fasting, practicing the austerity of the five fires (*pañcāgni-sādhana*), and entering beneath the earth—this is the quality of *tamas*. (2.6.33)
Performance with desire, the practice of yoga with desire, or the cessation of action through mere tranquility—this is the quality of *tamas*.
(2.6.34) The growing of nails, the growing of hair, holding up the hands, and vacuity of speech—this is the quality of *tamas*.
(2.6.35) Afflicting the body with various restraints, agitation caused by bodily suffering, and the mutilation of divine images out of anger—this is the quality of *tamas*. (2.6.36)
He who reviles the Divine is bound by worldly desires and is a doer of terrible deeds; he who does not cultivate the company of the virtuous is characterized by the quality of darkness (tamas).
2.6.37 Thus is this quality of darkness. Although it has been described at great length, this brief exposition has been made for the purpose of renouncing it.
2.6.38 He who conducts himself in this manner is possessed of the quality of darkness. This is the cause of downfall; through this, the attainment of liberation does not occur. 2.6.39
The entire fruit of an action performed under the influence of the quality of *tamas* is obtained; by that, the root of the suffering of birth is not severed.
(2.6.40) For the severance of the root of birth, the quality of *sattva* is necessary; its description will be given in the next section.
(2.6.41) Thus ends the sixth section in the second decade of the *Dāsabodha*.
Previously, the quality of *tamas* was described; it is the giver of suffering and is cruel. Now, listen to the quality of *sattva*. This is extremely difficult to attain.

(2.7.1) It is the foundation for devotion and the refuge of yogis. It casts away the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), which is the root of suffering. (2.7.2) By means of this, the supreme state is reached, the path toward the Blessed One is attained, and through it, liberation in union (*sāyujya-mukti*) is achieved. (2.7.3)
This is the protector of devotees; it is confidence within the ocean of worldly existence. That which is the state of the glory of liberation—that is this quality of *sattva*.

(2.7.4) That which is the ornament of the supreme truth, the adornment of the great ones, and by which the removal of *rajas* and *tamas* occurs—that is this quality of *sattva*. (2.7.5) That which brings about supreme happiness, and which, by bestowing a wave of bliss, wards off birth and death—that is this quality of *sattva*. (2.7.6)

That which is the end of ignorance, the foundational seat of merit, and by which the path to the next world is attained—that is this quality of *sattva*. (2.7.7) Such is this quality of *sattva*; when it manifests within the body of its own accord, its characteristic form of activity is as follows. (2.7.8) Excessive love for the Lord, regarding worldly affairs as merely mundane, and the constant presence of discernment—that is the quality of *sattva*. (2.7.9)
That which causes one to forget the suffering of *saṃsāra*, reveals the stainless path of devotion (*bhakti*), and generates the act of worship—that is the quality of *sattva*.

(2.7.10) Affection for the Supreme Truth (*paramārtha*), delight in the inner essence (*bhāvārtha*), and service to others—that is the quality of *sattva*. That is the quality of *sattva*. (2.7.11) Bathing, meritorious conduct such as the twilight prayers (*sandhyāvandana*), internal purity, and radiance in the body, clothing, and so forth—that is the quality of *sattva*. (2.7.12)

Performing sacrifices, officiating at sacrifices, studying, teaching, and performing meritorious acts of giving—whosoever does these himself possesses the quality of *sattva*. (2.7.13) Delight in discernment, a taste for the stories of Hari, and transformation through direct practice—this is the quality of *sattva*. (2.7.14) One who performs the gift of horses, the gift of elephants, the gift of cows, the gift of land, and the gift of various jewels possesses the quality of *sattva*. (2.7.15)
The giving of wealth, the giving of clothing, the giving of food, the giving of water, and the satisfying of Brahmins—he who performs these possesses the quality of *sattva*.

(2.7.16) The ritual bathing in Kārtika, the ritual bathing in Māgha, the observance of vows and their formal conclusion, charity, pilgrimage to sacred sites, and fasting—he who performs these without desire possesses the quality of *sattva*. (2.7.17) He who performs thousands of feasts, hundreds of thousands of feasts, and various kinds of gifts without desire possesses the quality of *sattva*; however, he who performs these very same acts with desire possesses the quality of *rajas*. (2.7.18)
He who offers land for a sacred site (*tīrtha*), constructs step-wells and lakes, and builds temples and spires—he possesses the quality of *sattva*.

(2.7.19) He who constructs a hall at the entrance of a temple, builds a flight of stairs, arranges rows of lamps, creates a grove (*vṛndāvana*), and builds a platform for the holy fig tree (*aśvattha*)—he possesses the quality of *sattva*.
(2.7.20) He who establishes forests and pleasure gardens, creates flower gardens, constructs water channels, and gladdens the hearts of ascetics—he possesses the quality of *sattva*. (2.7.21)
He who constructs twilight temples, subterranean passages, stairs on riverbanks, and storehouses at the gates of temples possesses the quality of *sattva*.
|| 2.7.22 || He who lights lamps for the various deities in their shrines and offers ornaments, decorations, and the like possesses the quality of *sattva*.

|| 2.7.23 || He who offers melodious musical instruments—such as the *jhallaṛī*, the *mṛdaṅga* drum, cymbals, the *ḍiṇḍima* drum, the kettledrum, and the *karṇikā* instrument—into the temple possesses the quality of *sattva*. || 2.7.24 ||
He who offers various kinds of beautiful literature in the temple, and he who is devoted to the worship of Hari—he possesses the quality of goodness (sattva-guṇa).
|| 2.7.25 || He who offers comfortable seats, palanquins, banners, flags, chowries, and special umbrellas in the temple—he possesses the quality of goodness (sattva-guṇa).
|| 2.7.26 || He who has a love for the construction of Vṛndāvana, the construction of decorative garlands, sweeping, and so forth—he possesses the quality of goodness (sattva-guṇa). || 2.7.27 ||
The dedication of various beautiful implements—such as pavilions, umbrellas, and seats—to the temple is the quality of goodness (sattvaguṇa). || 2.7.28 ||

He who offers various kinds of edible foods, various kinds of sacrificial offerings (naivedya), and unprecedented fruits for the sake of the Lord possesses the quality of goodness (sattva-guṇa). || 2.7.29 || Likewise, he whose delight is in devotion, who finds delight even in the service of a lowly servant, and who personally cleanses the gateway of the temple, possesses the quality of goodness. || 2.7.30 || He who finds joy in the lunar days (tithis), festival times (parvakāla), great celebrations (mahotsava), and so forth; and who offers everything through body, speech, and mind, possesses the quality of goodness. || 2.7.31 ||

He who is devoted to the stories of Hari and remains there constantly, having accepted its fragrance, garlands, and incense, possesses the quality of *sattva*. (2.7.32) Whether a man or a woman, he who stands at the temple gate having brought whatever materials he can afford possesses the quality of *sattva*.
(2.7.33) He who, setting aside even great worldly duties, hastens for the sake of the Lord’s work, and whose inner heart possesses such intense devotion, possesses the quality of *sattva*. (2.7.34)
He who stands at the gateway of the deity, having cast aside his own greatness from afar, and accepts even a lowly task there—that is the quality of *sattva*.

2.7.35 He who observes a fast for the sake of the deities, abstains from food, betel, and the like, and regularly practices recitation (*japa*), meditation (*dhyāna*), and so forth—that is the quality of *sattva*.
2.7.36 He who does not speak harsh words, conducts himself with extreme discipline, and by whom the yogis are satisfied—that is the quality of *sattva*. 2.7.37

He who, being free from pride, performs kīrtana without desire, and in whose kīrtana there arises the manifestation of perspiration and horripilation—he possesses the quality of *sattva*. 2.7.38 In whose mind there is meditation upon the Lord, by which his eyes become moist with tears and he forgets his own body—he possesses the quality of *sattva*. 2.7.39 He who has such great love for the stories of Hari that he never becomes weary of them; or he in whom love increases at the beginning or even at the end of the story—he possesses the quality of *sattva*. 2.7.40

He who has the name [of the Lord] on his mouth and cymbals in his hand, who describes the divine pastimes while dancing, and who bears the dust of the feet of devotees upon his head—he possesses the quality of *sattva*.

(2.7.41) He whose identification with the body has dissolved, whose detachment from sense objects has increased, and by whom the illusory nature of *māyā* has been realized—he possesses the quality of *sattva*.
(2.7.42) He who reflects in his mind that some means must be adopted and asks, "What is the use of attachment to the phenomenal world?"—he possesses the quality of *sattva*. (2.7.43)
He whose mind is terrified of *saṃsāra*, and in whose intellect the thought has arisen, "I shall perform some form of devotion," possesses the quality of *sattva*.

2.7.44 Even while remaining in his own stage of life (*āśrama*, i.e., the householder's), he who is respectful toward the eternal injunctions, and whose love is always fixed on Rāma, possesses the quality of *sattva*. 2.7.45 He who is anxious about everything, who dwells near the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), and in whom fortitude arises amidst afflictions, possesses the quality of *sattva*. 2.7.46
He who is always indifferent, who, being weary of various enjoyments, remembers the worship of the Blessed Lord—he possesses the quality of *sattva*.
2.7.47 He whose mind does not delight in worldly objects, who constantly remembers the Blessed Lord, and whose inner purpose is thus firm—he possesses the quality of *sattva*.
2.7.48 Even when people revile him, saying, "This man is eccentric," his love for the Lord increases all the more and his resolve becomes firmer—he possesses the quality of *sattva*. 2.7.49
That in which an inner vibration awakens, wherein reasoning becomes oriented toward one's true nature, and wherein faulty doubt ceases—that is the quality of *sattva*.
(2.7.50) The body may have its purpose; that in whose mind the desire for effort arises for that purpose is the quality of *sattva*.
(2.7.51) Peace, forbearance, compassion, and likewise certainty arise in him. Such is the function of the quality of *sattva*. (2.7.52)

Not sending away those guests who have arrived or come as visitors without having fed them; that which one gives according to one's ability is the quality of *sattva*. 2.7.53 If someone who is lowly, weak, or distressed comes to one’s own hermitage, providing a place for him is the quality of *sattva*. 2.7.54 Even if there is little food in one’s own house, not turning away [the guest] but always giving according to one's ability is the quality of *sattva*. 2.7.55
He who has conquered the tongue, whose latent impressions are satisfied, and who has no desire—that is the quality of *sattva*.
2.7.56 Through the reflection that "whatever is to be will be," his mind does not become restless even by worldly blows—that is the quality of *sattva*.
2.7.57 Having taken refuge in the one Blessed Lord, he by whom all (worldly) happiness has been renounced and even the body surrendered—that is the quality of *sattva*. 2.7.58

The latent impression (*vāsanā*) runs toward sense objects; nevertheless, that which remains unshakable, whose fortitude does not fail—that is the quality of *sattva*. (2.7.59) Whether the body is beset by calamity or afflicted by hunger and thirst, that whose resolve is firm—that is the quality of *sattva*.

(2.7.60) He by whom concentration has been attained through hearing, reflection, and meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*), and who has obtained pure self-knowledge—that is the quality of *sattva*. (2.7.61)
That in which egoism has perished, in which hopelessness shines, and in which compassion exists—that is the quality of *sattva*.

(2.7.62) He who behaves with humility toward all, who conducts himself according to moral bounds, and who satisfies all people—that is the quality of *sattva*. (2.7.63) He who possesses straightforwardness toward all beings, in whom even the mention of opposition does not exist, and who gives up even his own life for the sake of helping others—that is the quality of *sattva*. (2.7.64)

He who accomplishes the work of others even before his own, and whose fame remains after death, possesses the quality of *sattva*. (2.7.65) He who observes the virtues and faults of others but conceals them within himself like the ocean, possesses the quality of *sattva*.
(2.7.66) An inferior response must be endured, and no retort should be given to another; even if anger arises, it must be restrained—this is the quality of *sattva*. (2.7.67)
Even when people cause suffering and inflict various kinds of pain upon one unjustly, if one nevertheless endures it all within the mind, that is the quality of *sattva*.
2.7.68 Physical hardship must be endured; if one maintains friendship with the wicked and renders assistance even to those who revile, that is the quality of *sattva*.
2.7.69 When the mind wanders astray, if one restrains it through discernment and subdues the senses, that is the quality of *sattva*. 2.7.70

Virtuous action is to be practiced, evil action is to be abandoned, and the path of devotion is to be followed—this is the quality of *sattva*. (2.7.71) He who delights in the morning bath, who delights in listening to the Purāṇas, and who worships the deity with various mantras—he possesses the quality of *sattva*. (2.7.72) He who is diligent during festival times, intent upon the spring worship, and filled with great affection for birth-anniversary celebrations—he possesses the quality of *sattva*. (2.7.73)

If someone performs the final rites for a foreigner who has died, or if one is present at the time of the final rites, that is the quality of *sattva*. 2.7.74 If someone strikes another, and one goes there to restrain the striker and liberates living beings from bondage, that is the quality of *sattva*.

2.7.75 Offering a hundred thousand garlands to a Śiva-liṅga, faith in the consecration and the remembrance of the Name, and observing the rules for the vision of the Deity—this is the quality of *sattva*. 2.7.76
Upon seeing virtuous people, one hastens toward them; one is moved by supreme bliss and offers salutations with all one's being—this is the quality of *sattva*.
(2.7.77) In whom compassion for the virtuous arises, and by that compassion the upliftment of their lineage occurs—that portion of the Divine which is the quality of *sattva*.
(2.7.78) He who shows the path of truth to people, engages them in the worship of Hari, or speaks of knowledge—that is the quality of *sattva*. (2.7.79)

He for whom meritorious impressions (*puṇyasaṃskāra*) are pleasing, for whom circumambulation (*pradakṣiṇā*) is pleasing, for whom prostration (*namaskāra*) is pleasing, and whose oral recitation (*kaṇṭhapāṭha*) is firm—he possesses the quality of *sattva*. 2.7.80 He who has great devotion toward the object of worship, who collects a collection of texts, and who worships various metal images—he possesses the quality of *sattva*. 2.7.81 He whose ritual implements shine, and whose garlands, vessels, seats, garments, and purificatory items are likewise clean—he possesses the quality of *sattva*. 2.7.82

He who becomes sorrowful through the suffering of others, who becomes happy through the happiness of others, and who rejoices upon seeing detachment—that is the quality of *sattva*. 2.7.83 He who considers another’s ornament to be his own ornament, who considers another’s fault to be his own fault, and who is distressed by the suffering of others—that is the quality of *sattva*.
2.7.84 Enough with further elaboration now. He whose mind is directed toward the Divine and toward Dharma, and who practices dispassion—that is the quality of *sattva*. 2.7.85
Thus, this quality of *sattva* is by its very nature a deliverer from the ocean of *saṃsāra*. Through it, discernment regarding the path of knowledge arises.

(2.7.86) By means of the quality of *sattva*, devotion to the Blessed One is attained; by means of the quality of *sattva*, the attainment of knowledge is reached; and by means of the quality of *sattva*, liberation through union (*sāyujya-mukti*) is obtained.
(2.7.87) Such is the state of the quality of *sattva*. Regarding that, I have spoken briefly according to my understanding. May the listeners be attentive hereafter. (2.7.88)
Thus ends the seventh section, titled "The Quality of Goodness" (Sattvaguṇa).
This is the eighth section in the second decade.

Now, listen to the characteristics of the person of true knowledge (sadvidyā); these are supremely pure and auspicious marks. Through the investigation of these, true knowledge is attained. 2.8.1 In that person who possesses true knowledge, a distinction of the highest marks is seen; upon hearing of his virtues, there arises supreme satisfaction.
2.8.2 He is natural, sattvic, full of love, characterized by peace, forgiveness, and compassion, humble, devoted, and one whose speech is nectar-like. 2.8.3

He is supremely beautiful and skillful; he is supremely strong and steadfast; he is supremely accomplished and noble. 2.8.4 He is supremely wise and devoted; he is learned and dispassionate; he is a great ascetic and peaceful.
2.8.5 He is a speaker and free from desire; he is all-knowing (in listening to others) and respectful; he is excellent and humble in all things. 2.8.6

He is both a king and a righteous man; he is brave and discerning; he is youthful yet self-controlled. (2.8.7) He follows the conduct of the elders and adheres to the traditions of his lineage; his diet is balanced. He is free from agitation, a benefactor like Dhanvantari, and thus becomes illustrious.
(2.8.8) He is a performer of duty without pride; he is both a singer and a devotee of Viṣṇu. Though possessed of great wealth, he remains devoted to the worship of the Lord. (2.8.9)

He is both a knower of reality and remains equanimous; though deeply learned, he is a virtuous person; and though a counselor, he is endowed with excellence and moral conduct. 2.8.10 Supreme delight in the subject of the ultimate truth, following the path of the righteous, the performance of noble deeds, concentration, fortitude, study of the Vedas, study of the Smṛtis, hearing the pastimes of the Lord, reasoning according to the scriptures, praise of the Lord, intelligence, and critical examination—these qualities reside in him. 2.8.12

He is skillful, clever, competent, a logician, truthful, literary, disciplined, a knower of the vital points, dexterous, agile, and possessed of various wonders. 2.8.13 He is respectful, appreciative of honor, a knower of degrees of excellence, skilled in application, aware of the proper occasion, attentive to the context, a knower of the signs of cause and effect, discerning, and an eloquent speaker. 2.8.14 He is vigilant, critical, effective, a purifier of traditional scriptures, an awakener of theoretical and practical knowledge, and decisive. 2.8.15
He becomes one who performs preparatory rites, a dweller at sacred fords, firm in his vows, an ascetic who subjects the body to hardship, a lay devotee, and a master of self-restraint.
2.8.16 He is always truthful in speech, auspicious in speech, gentle in speech, consistent in speech, decisive in speech, pleasant in speech, and speaks with happiness.
2.8.17 He is one whose desires are satisfied, profound, a yogi, noble-minded, serene, free from passion, gentle, virtuous by nature, following the pure path, guileless, and free from vice. 2.8.18

He is one who delights in well-composed music, who perceives virtues, who is free from expectations, who wins over the world, who is upright, and who is full of loving-kindness toward all beings. (2.8.19) He is pure in his possessions, pure in his wife, pure in his conduct, pure within, pure in his engagement with the world, pure in his withdrawal from it, and pure in every respect.

(2.8.20) Through the cultivation of loving-kindness, he brings about the welfare of others; through the sweetness of his speech, he removes the sorrow of others; through his capability, he wields the rod of justice; and through his personal effort, he establishes friendliness toward the world. (2.8.21)

He is the dispeller of doubt and possesses a broad mouth; even though he is omniscient, he becomes a listener to others. In explaining a discourse, he does not convey words devoid of their intended meaning. (2.8.22)

He becomes virtuous, pure, and of holy character. He is one whose mind is cleansed, whose soul is rooted in dharma, compassionate, devoted to action, stainless through the performance of his own duty, free from greed, and full of remorse for past faults. He engages in discourse that is free from contention. He is unattached and free from limiting conditions. He is devoid of evil desires, free from anger, faultless, and without envy. 2.8.23 He is resolute, possessed of stainless knowledge, and composed; he is also a devotee. Though he is a perfected one (*siddha*), he maintains his spiritual practice as if he were still a seeker (*sādhaka*). 2.8.24
He possesses a beautiful form, the form of contentment, the form of bliss, the form of laughter, the form of unity, and he exists as the Self within all.
2.8.25 He becomes fortunate, victorious, handsome, virtuous, well-conducted, active, and reflective.
2.8.26 He becomes illustrious, renowned, powerful, capable, heroic, a bestower of boons, truthful, and a doer of good deeds. 2.8.27

He is possessed of knowledge, skilled in the arts, endowed with auspicious marks, of noble lineage, pure, strong, and compassionate. 2.8.28 He is resourceful, virtuous, excellent, intelligent, very steadfast, initiated, always contented, free from craving, and devoid of passion. 2.8.29 Let it be so; such indeed are the characteristics of true knowledge (sadvidyā). This has been described in brief for the sake of practice. 2.8.30

Neither physical beauty nor charm is attainable through practice; innate qualities are not obtainable by means of effort. Therefore, let there be at least some practice toward adventitious virtues. (2.8.31) This is that supreme true knowledge (*sadvidyā*); it is possible for all, but it should be practiced especially by one who is dispassionate.
(2.8.32) Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Exposition of True Knowledge."

Now, listen to the characteristics of one who is dispassionate (*virakta*). Listen to what virtues arise in the dispassionate one, by which that yogi may attain his true capability. (2.9.1) By these virtues, good fame spreads far and wide; by them, life becomes meaningful; and by them, the dispassionate attain greatness. (2.9.2) Through these, the dispassionate one finds the opportunity for the supreme goal (*paramārtha*); the bliss of the dispassionate one surges forth; and dispassion, when accompanied by discernment (*viveka*), becomes twofold. (2.9.3)
Through these, happiness arises, true knowledge becomes clear, the glory of fortune becomes powerful, and liberation is accomplished.
(2.9.4) Through these, desires are fulfilled, all longings become complete, and Sarasvatī, the progenitor of sweet sounds, dwells within the mouth.
(2.9.5) These characteristics should be heard and firmly internalized; by that, one becomes detached and renowned throughout the world. (2.9.6)
One who is dispassionate shall become discerning; one who is dispassionate shall expound upon the supreme self; one who is dispassionate shall maintain fortitude regarding self-restraint.
(2.9.7) One who is dispassionate shall protect the means [to liberation]; one who is dispassionate shall engage in devotion; one who is dispassionate shall manifest the specific knowledge of Brahman.
(2.9.8) One who is dispassionate shall increase devotion; one who is dispassionate shall demonstrate peace; one who is dispassionate shall, with effort, preserve his own dispassion. (2.9.9)
One who is dispassionate should establish virtuous action; one who is dispassionate should expand renunciation; one who is dispassionate should maintain hopelessness with firmness.
(2.9.10) One who is dispassionate should establish righteousness; one who is dispassionate should rely upon policy; one who is dispassionate should observe forgiveness with great care.

(2.9.11) One who is dispassionate should illuminate the supreme truth; one who is dispassionate should purify inquiry; one who is dispassionate should preserve the true path and the quality of goodness within his presence. (2.9.12)

One who is dispassionate should observe those who are potential followers; one who is dispassionate should satisfy those who are full of love; one who is dispassionate should not neglect potential followers who have come for refuge.
|| 2.9.13 || One who is dispassionate should be supremely skillful; one who is dispassionate should be an internal witness; one who is dispassionate should uphold the side of the ultimate truth.

|| 2.9.14 || One who is dispassionate should practice; one who is dispassionate should exert long-term effort; one who is dispassionate should, through verbal artistry, reconcile even the ultimate truth that has been broken. || 2.9.15 ||

One who is dispassionate shall speak pure knowledge; one who is dispassionate shall praise detachment; one who is dispassionate shall achieve unwavering concentration. (2.9.16) One who is dispassionate shall perform great festivals on sacred days; one who is dispassionate shall sustain the circles of devotees; one who is dispassionate shall, with great effort, sustain the paths of worship endowed with splendor. (2.9.17) One who is dispassionate shall perform the chanting of Hari’s names; one who is dispassionate shall propagate exposition; one who is dispassionate shall cause revilers and wicked people to feel shame by means of the foundation of the path of devotion. (2.9.18)
One who is dispassionate should perform service to others in many ways; he should increase virtuous deeds and expand the path of merit through his strength.
(2.9.19) Bathing, the twilight prayers, recitation, meditation, pilgrimage to sacred sites, devotion to the Lord, self-restraint, purity, and a pure mind—these belong to the dispassionate one.
(2.9.20) The dispassionate one should possess firm resolve. He should move through the world with ease, yet by mere association, he should effect the upliftment of people. (2.9.21)
One who is dispassionate should be steadfast; one who is dispassionate should be noble; one who is dispassionate should be intent upon the object of discernment.

||2.9.22|| One who is dispassionate should be skillful; one who is dispassionate should tread the pure path; one who is dispassionate, having himself become diminished [of worldly existence], should leave behind only his fame.

||2.9.23|| One who is dispassionate should seek out the dispassionate; one who is dispassionate should recognize the virtuous; one who is dispassionate should form friendship with virtuous yogis. ||2.9.24||

The dispassionate one should perform preparatory rites (*puraścaraṇa*). The dispassionate one should undertake pilgrimages to sacred sites. The dispassionate one should create various beautiful places. (2.9.25) The dispassionate one may assume external adjuncts (*upādhi*), yet he must not abandon the state of supreme indifference; he should have no evil desire regarding any object whatsoever. (2.9.26) The dispassionate one should be established within himself. The dispassionate one should not fail in his duties. The dispassionate one should not be inferior due to dependence on others. (2.9.27)

One who is dispassionate shall be a knower of the rules; one who is dispassionate shall be a knower of proper association; one who is dispassionate shall be skillful in every respect. (2.9.28) One who is dispassionate shall not be partial; one who is dispassionate shall practice everything; one who is dispassionate shall understand everything exactly as it is. (2.9.29) Discourse on Hari, philosophical exposition, worship with attributes (*saguṇa-bhajana*), knowledge of Brahman, knowledge of the physical body (*piṇḍa-jñāna*), and knowledge of reality (*tattva-jñāna*)—one who is dispassionate shall know all this. (2.9.30)

One who is dispassionate should know in their entirety the path of action, the path of worship, the path of knowledge, the path of established conclusions, the path of worldly engagement, and the path of renunciation. (2.9.31) One who is dispassionate should know all of this: the state of love, the state of indifference, the state of yoga, the state of meditation, the state of the bodiless, and the state of spontaneity. (2.9.32) Having observed sounds, gestures, targets, postures, mantras, diagrams, injunctions, ritual procedures, and the various philosophical systems, one should relinquish them all. (2.9.33)
The dispassionate one shall be a friend to the world; the dispassionate one shall be independent; the dispassionate one shall possess manifold virtues.
|| 2.9.34 || The dispassionate one is indeed truly dispassionate; the dispassionate one shall be a devotee of Hari; the dispassionate one, through being untainted, shall be eternally liberated.

|| 2.9.35 || The dispassionate one shall study the scriptures; the dispassionate one shall refute [false] doctrines; the dispassionate one shall establish those seeking liberation on the true path. || 2.9.36 ||
One who is dispassionate should establish others on the pure path; one who is dispassionate should cut through doubt; one who is dispassionate should regard all people as his own kin.

2.9.37 One who is dispassionate should honor those who revile him; one who is dispassionate should instruct those who practice spiritual discipline; one who is dispassionate should awaken those bound by their investigation of seekers of liberation.

2.9.38 One who is dispassionate should adopt virtuous qualities; one who is dispassionate should abandon base qualities; one who is dispassionate should ward off various calamities through the power of discernment. 2.9.39

Thus, these supreme characteristics should be heard with a one-pointed mind; one who is detached should not disregard them. 2.9.40 This much has been said in brief; thereafter, one should accept as much as is pleasing. Listeners should not find fault by thinking, "Too much has been said. 2.9.41 For if the supreme characteristics are not accepted and inferior characteristics prevail, the "wisdom" of fools comes into play. 2.9.42
The characteristics of that fool-scholar have been described in the following summary; they should be heard with careful attention.
Thus ends the ninth summary, titled "The Characteristics of the Dispassionate."

The characteristics previously described bring about cleverness even in fools. Now, listen to the characteristics of those who are wise yet foolish; they are known as "foolish-wise" (mūrkhapaṇḍita). The listeners should not feel dejection here, for happiness is attained by abandoning faults. He who is highly learned and accomplished, who speaks clearly of the knowledge of Brahman, yet harbors false hopes and pride in his heart—he is a "foolish-wise" man.

He who advocates the abandonment of action, who destroys qualified devotion (*saguṇabhakti*), and who censures one’s own duty (*svadharma*) and the means of practice (*sādhana*), is a fool-scholar. (2.10.4) He who, on the basis of his own knowledge, reviles everyone and looks upon every living being as deficient, is a fool-scholar. (2.10.5) His speech is that of a fool-scholar if it leads to the occasion of disregarding a disciple, or if it places him in danger, or if it causes the discouragement of people’s minds. (2.10.6)
He who is full of passion (*rajas*), full of darkness (*tamas*), deceitful, and crooked in his inner heart; he who, upon seeing wealth, offers praise—he is a fool-scholar (2.10.7).
He who, without even having examined a book from beginning to end, seeks to find fault with it; who, when a merit is mentioned, perceives only a defect—he is a fool-scholar (2.10.8).
He who becomes agitated upon hearing of auspicious qualities, who acts out of envy, and who, under the influence of arrogance, disregards words of prudent conduct—he is a fool-scholar (2.10.9).
He who engages in action out of the conceit of being a knower, he who is unable to restrain his anger, or he for whom there is a discrepancy between his words and his deeds—he is a fool-scholar.
(2.10.10) He who exerts himself by giving explanations without qualification, and whose speech is harsh—he is a fool-scholar.
(2.10.11) He who is a listener well-versed in many scriptures yet is talkative, and who points out the deficiencies of the listener—he is a fool-scholar. (2.10.12)
"He who does not realize that 'whatever faults I uproot in others, those same faults exist in me as well' is a fool-scholar.
(2.10.13) "Even one who has reached the further shore of all branches of knowledge through the power of practice, yet is unable to bring about the mental composure of people, is a fool-scholar.
(2.10.14) "Just as an elephant is bound by a thread of wool, and just as a bee dies in a lotus out of greed, so too is he who is attached to the phenomenal world a fool-scholar. (2.10.15)

He who associates with women, he who forms attachments to women, and he who accepts what is censurable—he is a fool-scholar (mūrkhapaṇḍita). || 2.10.16 He who firmly holds in his mind that which would lead to his own downfall, and he who possesses the notion of identifying with the body—he is a fool-scholar.
|| 2.10.17 That man who, setting aside the Lord of Śrī, praises human beings, or else praises every person he encounters—he is a fool-scholar. || 2.10.18

He who describes the limbs of women, who mimics their various gestures and emotional states, and who forgets God—he is a fool-scholar (mūrkhapaṇḍita). ||2.10.19|| He who, out of pride in his own power, considers every living being insignificant, and who propounds the doctrine of nihilism—he is a fool-scholar.
||2.10.20|| He who, though highly learned, free from passion, a knower of Brahman, and a great yogi, nevertheless tells people about the future—he is a fool-scholar. ||2.10.21||
One who, upon hearing the name of someone, contemplates that person's virtues or faults in his mind, and feels envy toward the ornaments of others, is a fool-scholar (mūrkhapaṇḍita).

|| 2.10.22 || One who possesses neither the practice of devotion, nor dispassion, nor worship, and who speaks of the knowledge of Brahman without ritual action, is a fool-scholar (mūrkhapaṇḍita). || 2.10.23 ||

He who does not respect sacred fords (*tīrtha*), does not respect holy fields (*puṇyakṣetra*), does not respect the Vedas, and does not respect the scriptures; and he who, though born into a pure family, is impure—he is a fool-scholar (*mūrkhapaṇḍita*). (2.10.24) Seeing respect shown toward his own domain, he takes delight therein; even if that person has no reputation, he offers praise, yet at that very moment he disparages him with contempt—he is a fool-scholar. (2.10.25) He whose conduct is such that he says one thing while doing another—he is a fool-scholar. (2.10.26)

He who has attachment for the realm of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) and lacks regard for the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), who, being a knower, resorts to ignorance—he is a fool-scholar (2.10.27).
He who abandons truthful speech and speaks with a deceitful mind, whose life is dependent on others—he is a fool-scholar (2.10.28).
He who displays the appearance of goodness on the surface but practices what is forbidden, who follows that very path by force even while walking on the wrong path—he is a fool-scholar (2.10.29).

He who, even after listening day and night, does not abandon his own faults and does not recognize what is for his own welfare—he is a fool-scholar. (2.10.30) He who, ignoring the virtuous people who have come to hear his exposition, speaks instead by focusing on petty individuals—he is a fool-scholar. (2.10.31) He who, out of greed, desires to keep as a disciple even one who has fallen from his position and who treats him with contempt—he is a fool-scholar. (2.10.32)

If, at the time of investigation, bodily pain arises and one becomes angry, he is a fool-scholar (mūrkhapaṇḍita). || 2.10.33 || He who, intoxicated by his own power and wealth, neglects the true guru and conceals the lineage of his own gurus, is a fool-scholar. || 2.10.34 || He who speaks of knowledge with his mouth but accomplishes only his own self-interest, who accumulates wealth like a miser, and who speaks of the supreme truth for the sake of profit—he is a fool-scholar. || 2.10.35 ||

He who, without practicing it himself, teaches others, and expounds the knowledge of Brahman for the sake of worldly gain—he who, though being virtuous, is dependent on others, is a fool-scholar (mūrkhapaṇḍita).
|| 2.10.36 || He who performs such actions by which the path of devotion is broken and by which his own hypocrisy is made manifest—he is a fool-scholar.

|| 2.10.37 || He for whom the phenomenal world that was in his hands has vanished, yet by whom not even a trace of the supreme truth has been attained, and who hates the gods and the brahmins—he is a fool-scholar. || 2.10.38 ||

The characteristics of the fool and the wise man have been stated for the purpose of abandoning faults. In this regard, the discerning should forgive any deficiency or excess [in the description]. 2.10.39 He who considers this world to be happiness is the fool among even the most foolish, because there is no other suffering equal to the suffering of this worldly existence. 2.10.40 That very point is explained further below. The dwelling in the womb, which is the characteristic form of the suffering of birth, is described next. 2.10.41
Thus ends the tenth section of the second chapter, titled "The Definition of the Characteristics of the Fool and the Wise."

Birth is indeed the sprout of suffering; birth is indeed the ocean of sorrow; birth is indeed the steadfast mountain of fear. (3.1.1) Birth is indeed the crucible for karmas; birth is indeed the mine of evils; birth is indeed the ever-new affliction of time.
(3.1.2) Birth is indeed the fruit of false knowledge; birth is indeed the lotus of greed; birth is indeed the film of delusion produced by ignorance. (3.1.3)

Saṃsāra is the root of suffering; therein, one is consumed by pain. First, the agony experienced in the womb was described. 3.2.1 The suffering endured during residence in the womb is forgotten by the infant. Subsequently, that infant grows day by day. 3.2.2 The skin of an infant is tender; when there is pain, the infant suffers. At that time, there is no speech; he is unable to manifest happiness or suffering. 3.2.3

An infant is not capable of protecting his own body; therefore, various calamities occur. At times he acts like a vagrant, whereby some limb becomes deformed. (3.2.8) Or, perhaps due to the power of past merit, no calamities occur; then, day by day, the infant recognizes his mother.
(3.2.9) If he does not see his mother for even a moment, he cries out in distress. At that time, there is no person whatsoever who is equal to a mother. (3.2.10)
He awaits his mother with longing; he never finds delight without his mother. When he remembers her, he cannot endure even a moment’s separation from her.
(3.2.11) Even if the gods beginning with Brahmā should come, or even if Lakṣmī herself were to look upon him, he would not find peace without his mother.
(3.2.12) Whether she be of low birth, ill-favored, or even destitute, there is no one on the face of the earth equal to a mother. (3.2.13)

Thus, without his mother, he is forlorn; without his mother, he is incomplete. Even if she drives him away in anger, he cries out and embraces her alone. 3.2.14 In the presence of his mother, he finds happiness; when she has gone far away, he becomes distressed. At that time, his affection for his mother is most intense. 3.2.15 Then the mother died. The child became orphaned. Crying out "Mother! Mother!", the boy grew emaciated. 3.2.16

The mother is not within the range of his vision; he gazes upon people with wretchedness. The hope that "my mother will come" dwells in his mind. (3.2.17) Thinking it might be his mother, he looks toward someone's face; but realizing, "This is not my mother," he becomes one whose hopes are destroyed and is dejected. (3.2.18) Having encountered suffering through separation from his mother, there is an experience of grief in the mind, and even the body has become utterly emaciated. (3.2.19)

Alternatively, if the mother was well-protected, she and her offspring lived together; consequently, day by day, the state of childhood passed away. (3.2.20) Childhood is characterized by laughter, and as cleverness increased day by day, the intense affection that had existed for the mother became diminished.
(3.2.21) Subsequently, delight in play increased, a circle of companions was gathered, and joy and sorrow arose from the cycles of coming and going in games. (3.2.22)
The parents cause him to study with the utmost persistence; consequently, the child experiences supreme suffering. The habit formed through association with his playmates is not abandoned.

(3.2.23) In playing with other children, he does not remember his mother, nor his father. Even during play, he occasionally encounters sudden pain. (3.2.24) A tooth falls out, an eye is injured, a foot is broken, deformity ensues, intoxication fades, and a state of wretchedness is reached. (3.2.25)

A fever of chills has arrived, or a fever of smallpox; a headache has arisen; a fever has come on; or a constant colic has been initiated in the abdomen by wind. 3.2.26 An affliction by spirits has occurred; an affliction by a water-deity has occurred; he has been seized by *muñja*, *khoṭiṅga*, *haṃsa*, or *bādī* [spirits]. 3.2.27 He has been seized by *vetālas*, *khaṅkālas*, *brahmapaiśācas*, and so forth; or else, an offering (*bali*) that should not have been transgressed has been transgressed. 3.2.28

Some said, "He has been seized by Vīradeva. Others said, "He has been seized by Khaṇḍerāva. Still others said, "All of this is false; he has been seized by a *brahmarākṣasa*. (3.2.29) Some said, "A deity has been invoked within him through some form of sorcery (*abhicāra*). Others said, "An error occurred during the propitiation of the goddess Saṭavāī. (3.2.30) Some said, "This is the ripening of his past karma (*karmabhoga*); various diseases have arisen in his body. Then, excellent physicians were summoned. (3.2.31)
Some say, "He will not live"; others say, "He will not die. Due to the power of past misdeeds, he experiences various kinds of suffering.

(3.2.32) That living being by whom the suffering of the womb was forgotten is now tormented by the threefold fires; he has experienced great hardship through the suffering of *saṃsāra*. (3.2.33) Even if he were released from all these sufferings, he would still be awakened by repeated blows. From the perspective of worldly convention, he has become so clever that he has preserved the greatness of his lineage. (3.2.34)

Then, out of haste born from parental affection for their son, the parents made preparations for his marriage; they displayed all their wealth and settled the bride. (3.2.35) Having witnessed the splendor of the wedding and the assembly of kinsmen, he experienced supreme happiness; his heart became attached to the house of his father-in-law alone.
(3.2.36) "Let my parents be as they may; I shall go to the house of my father-in-law well-attired. For that purpose, he even incurs debt through various pretexts. (3.2.37)

There is an internal feeling of affection toward the father-in-law’s house in every respect; the poor parents are entirely distressed for this reason. That alone is their concern. He does not give them the fruit of their affection. (3.2.38) When the daughter-in-law enters the house, he becomes excessively attached; he thinks that there is no one like me. (3.2.39)

Deprived of their wives, [men] become insignificant (neglected) by their mothers, fathers, brothers, and sisters. Deluded by ignorance in the form of sin, this man is excessively attached to his wife. 3.2.40 Even in the absence of sexual union, there is such great affection; but when union occurs, it becomes boundless. Then that affection increases, and consequently, the living being becomes bound by the noose of desire. 3.2.41 If she is out of sight for even a moment, his life-force becomes restless. She, the object of his affection, draws him into her innermost heart. 3.2.42
Her soft and charming sounds, her restrained conduct, her sense of modesty, her lotus-like face, and the glance from her eyes—all of this is indeed a snare of desire.

(3.2.43) The impulse of desire cannot be restrained; the body, rendered agitated by the pursuit of desire, cannot be controlled; the mind finds no delight in any other endeavor; and there is constant unease within the heart. (3.2.44)

He performs external activities, yet his mind remains fixed only on his home; moment by moment, he remembers that beloved woman within his heart. (3.2.45) Having said, "You are the very life of my life," she displays her skill in amorous passion and thus captivates his mind.
(3.2.46) The deceitful first display an outward connection, but thereafter they take away one's life with their snares; such is the condition of this person at the end of his life. (3.2.47)
(Desire gives pleasure at first, but in the end it takes away one's life. He feels such an attachment for his beloved that if anyone should become angry with her, distress arises in his mind.
(3.2.48) Out of partiality for his wife, he speaks disparaging words to his mother and father; having insulted them, he separates himself from them. (3.2.49)
For the sake of a woman, shame was abandoned; for the sake of a woman, friends were abandoned; for the sake of a woman, all kinsmen were abandoned.

(3.2.50) For the sake of a woman, the body was sold; for the sake of a woman, the status of a servant was accepted; for the sake of a woman, discernment was lost. (3.2.51) For the sake of a woman, lewdness was accepted; for the sake of a woman, excessive subservience was accepted; for the sake of a woman, dependence on others was accepted. (3.2.52)

On account of a woman, he became greedy; on account of a woman, he abandoned righteousness (*dharma*). On account of a woman, he avoided pilgrimage to sacred sites (*tīrthayātrā*); on account of a woman, he lost his own duty (*svadharma*).
(3.2.53) On account of a woman, he did not, in any way, contemplate what is auspicious or inauspicious. Whether body, mind, or wealth—everything was surrendered to the woman with undivided devotion.

(3.2.54) On account of a woman, the supreme goal (*paramārtha*) was submerged; his own welfare was sacrificed. His focus regarding the Lord (*Īśvara*) was contracted, and instead, on account of a woman, he became attached to sensual desire (*kāma*). (3.2.55)

Devotion was renounced for the sake of a woman; detachment was manifested for the sake of a woman; even liberation through union (*sāyujya-mukti*) was spurned for the sake of a woman. (3.2.56) The entire universe was considered trivial for the sake of a woman; even those as dear as one's own life-breath were deemed wicked for her sake. (3.2.57) Thus, his inner affection was firmly bound [to her], and by that he lost everything. Then, suddenly, that wife died. (3.2.58)

Grief arose in his mind: "He says, 'This is a great calamity; now my entire world has utterly perished. For her sake, I abandoned the company of my kinsmen; now, all at once, my home is shattered. Now I am abandoning this wife"—thus he wailed in sorrow. (3.2.59) Embracing the woman's corpse, he beats his chest and beats his belly. Without shame, he sings of her virtues in the presence of the people. (3.2.61)

Then he says, "My house is ruined; now I shall never again exist in this world. Thus, with great sorrow, he began a terrible lamentation. (3.2.62) His life-force was agitated by her death; he recoiled from everything. Through that suffering, he became either a yogi or a high-souled being. (3.2.63) Or else, instead of renouncing the world, he married again; consequently, his mind became utterly absorbed in his second wife. (3.2.64)
The second marriage took place; once again, joy arose. The listeners should hear the following section with careful attention.
Thus ends the second section, titled "The Examination of the Qualified," in the *Śrī Dāsabodha*, a dialogue between Guru and Disciple.
The second marriage was accomplished; by it, his former suffering was forgotten, and he lived considering worldly existence to be happiness. 3.3.1

He has become utterly miserly; he does not even eat sufficient food. For the sake of every single grain, he would even give up his life. (3.3.2) Even when the end of the eon has arrived, he makes no expenditure; instead, he accumulates again and again. How could there be a virtuous latent impression within such a person? (3.3.3) He does not practice righteousness himself, and he even prevents others from practicing it. He constantly reviles virtuous people. (3.3.4)
He knows not the sacred ford, nor does he know the vow; he does not honor the guest, nor does he honor the visitor. Having gathered even a single grain from the mouth of an ant, he accumulates it.
(3.3.5) He does not perform merit himself, nor can he bear to see what has been done by another. "This [action] does not bring satisfaction," he says, mocking merit.
(3.3.6) He destroys both gods and devotees; by his physical strength, he oppresses everyone; with harsh words, he breaks the hearts of living beings. (3.3.7)
Having cast policy far away, he conducts himself with injustice; he remains perpetually bloated with pride.
(3.3.8) His ancestors have been deceived; no funeral rites were performed for them, nor was a *śrāddha* offered. Even the family deity has been cheated. Such is the case.

(3.3.9) Thinking, "She is well-dressed," his own sister was invited for a meal. When her maternal uncle arrived to take her [home], he too was invited for a meal under the pretext that he was a Brahmin. (3.3.10)
He never takes pleasure in stories of Hari; he avoids the Lord in every way. He says, "Bathing and the twilight prayers are useless; why should they be performed?
(3.3.11) Out of desire, he accumulates wealth; for that purpose, he commits treachery. In his youth, he became intoxicated with pride.
(3.3.12) Youth flourished within his body, but there was no fortitude; thus, he committed a great sin and an improper act. (3.3.13)

A second marriage was contracted, yet the wife was of tender age. It was impossible to restrain the mind in any way. Through attachment to sensual objects, the distinction between the familiar and the unfamiliar vanished. (3.3.14) He took no account of his mother, nor did he take account of his sister. He committed adultery with another's wife. Consequently, he was punished in the royal court; nevertheless, he did not desist. (3.3.15) When another's wife came within the range of his vision, desire arose in his mind. Thereupon, he performed an improper act, and because of that, he experienced suffering once again. (3.3.16)
Thus, excessive evil was committed; therein, neither the auspicious nor the inauspicious was considered. By those faults, the body was suddenly seized by disease.
(3.3.17) Every limb was pervaded by maladies; the living being was assailed by consumption. His own committed sin was experienced in the form of suffering almost immediately.
(3.3.18) By the disease, every limb was shattered; the nose became sunken; his auspicious marks vanished, and his ill-omened traits were revealed. (3.3.19)

The body has become emaciated; various afflictions have arisen; the strength of youth has departed; the living being has in every way reached a state of frailty. (3.3.20) Pain has manifested in all limbs; the body is impaired; devoid of power, the living being trembles violently. (3.3.21) The hands and feet have withered away; worms have been born in all the limbs; seeing this, people—from children to the elderly—have begun to spit. (3.3.22)

Diarrhea has set in; a foul odor has arisen on all sides; the living being has become exceedingly emaciated; now his life cannot be preserved. (3.3.23) "Now, O Lord, grant me death! Much suffering has been endured by this life; the accumulation of my sins has not yet reached its end," (3.3.24) thus he weeps bitterly with grief. Whenever he looks upon his own body, then and there, becoming distressed, this wretched man suffers in agony. (3.3.25)
Thus much suffering arose; everything was destroyed as if struck by the wind, and his wealth was forcibly plundered by thieves.

(3.3.26) In this way, neither this world nor the next was secured; a strange fate has arrived, such that he himself had to consume his own excrement and urine. (3.3.27) (At that point) the collection of evils came to an end; because of that, his daily agony diminished. A physician administered medicine, and treatment was established. (3.3.28)

As if rescued from death, his rebirth has occurred. People said, "He has entered among men once again. (3.3.29) A new wife was brought home; the worldly life began once more; that self-interested mind was accepted yet again. (3.3.30) Some wealth was acquired; again, a collection of possessions was made. Yet, because there was no offspring, it was as if the house were lost. (3.3.31)

He became sorrowful, thinking, "I have no son. The world spread the ill repute that he was "barren" (*vandhya*). He reflected, "May this ill repute perish; for that purpose, let there be a lineage through a daughter. (3.3.32) For that end, he made resolutions and performed various efforts. Pilgrimages, vows, fasts, the holding [of breath], the breaking of the fast, and other such means were undertaken. (3.3.33)

Worldly pleasures were far off; rather, suffering was obtained due to their barrenness. Nevertheless, the deity became pleased, and by that means, offspring was born. (3.3.34) The parents felt exceeding affection for that child. They did not let him remain even a single moment away from them. When suffering befell him, both of them wailed aloud. (3.3.35) In their distress, they worshipped various deities for his well-being. Meanwhile, due to the force of his past karma, his death occurred. (3.3.36)

Because of that, much suffering arose; grief was born in the home. The two of them said, "Why has our childlessness been ordained by fate? What is the use of wealth to us? Let it go to others, but let there be offspring. For the sake of offspring, we would renounce everything. "Our childlessness has now passed away, but in its place, the state of having stillborn children has arrived. That cannot be destroyed by any means whatsoever"—thus they cried out loudly in sorrow.
"Why has the creeper of our lineage been cut down? Alas! Our domestic way of life is lost; has the mistress of the house been provoked, so that the lamp of the family has been extinguished?

3.3.40 "Now, if I may behold the face of my offspring, I shall joyfully perform the *agnidivya* (the ordeal by fire). Likewise, in the presence of the mistress of the house, I shall observe the vow of [touching] the throat with a thorn. 3.3.41

O Mother of the World, I shall employ my son in your service; I shall give him the name "Kerapuñja. Upon his nose, I shall wear an ornament bearing your name; please fulfill this supreme desire of my heart. (3.3.42) Many vows were made directed toward many deities; many virtuous men were sought after; and many scorpions were swallowed. (3.3.43)
A ritual worship was performed; the deities were invoked and made to circulate within her body. Plantains, coconuts, and mangoes were given to the Brahmins.
(For the sake of a son,) various crooked rites were practiced and numerous vows and resolutions were undertaken, yet the unseen power remained adverse; therefore, no son was born.
For the sake of a son, she bathed at the foot of trees, by which even the fruit-bearing trees were scorched. Thus, out of longing for a son, she committed various harmful acts.

Many have condemned sense-objects, yet they have also indulged in them; for indeed, the maintenance of the body is not possible without the enjoyment of sense-objects. 12.7.2 To say that one thing is in words while another is in actions is called a deficient discrimination; by this, one becomes an object of ridicule in the world. 12.7.3 Statements are seen here and there that the next world cannot be attained without the renunciation of sense-objects. 12.7.4
The worldly ones eat; do those who seek the ultimate truth subsist on fasting? Regarding the objects of the senses, equality is seen in both cases.

12.7.5 One may eat what one desires oneself; the remaining food should be distributed. However, there is no such rule that one must waste food. 12.10.1 Likewise, the practitioner should be satisfied with knowledge; he should speak that very knowledge to others. He who is capable of crossing over should rescue the person who is drowning. 2
(The practitioner) should personally adopt the highest virtues and speak of those virtues to many people. It is improper to speak to others without practicing them oneself. 3.

Bathing, the twilight prayers (*saṃdhyāvandana*), worship of the deity, recitation (*japa*), meditation (*dhyāna*), and the narration of the stories of Hari should be performed with a one-pointed mind. 4.
One should employ the body for the benefit of others; one should provide assistance in the work of many; and one should make an effort so that there is no deficiency in anyone's work. 5.
One should recognize people who are attached or oppressed and act for their benefit to the best of one's ability. One should speak with gentle words to everyone.

(The practitioner) should be pained by the suffering of others and delighted by the happiness of others. One should win over all living beings with virtuous words. Many people commit injustice; one should be patient toward them. Many tasks must be performed; through this, those who are strangers will become like one's own kin. 12.10.8

One must know the mind of another and act in accordance with it; one must examine people in various ways. 12.10.9 (The practitioner) should speak with restraint and give a reply at the appropriate time; always abandoning anger by relying on patience. 10. One must completely abandon laziness and exert great effort; one must not yield to the verbal deceptions of anyone. 11.

(The practitioner) should give the best object to another; he should speak after reflecting on his words; he should conduct worldly affairs with mindfulness. 12 May there be remembrance of death; may there be reverence for devotion to Hari; thus, even after death, let one's fame remain.
13 Many people know him who conducts himself according to discipline; for him who acts with integrity in all matters, what can be lacking? 14

He who is distinguished by such supreme qualities is alone called a *puruṣa* (true person). By his devotion, the Supreme Self becomes satisfied. (15) Some people, having uttered much reproach, speak [against him]; nevertheless, his own peace shall not be lost. Those who live even among the wicked without conflict are virtuous and blessed.
(16) He who is adorned with supreme qualities and graced by knowledge and dispassion—he alone is the best person on the face of the earth. 12.10.17
One must personally undertake hardship; one must endure much. Even if one becomes exhausted by various means oneself, one’s reputation must be preserved.

(The practitioner) if he desires pleasure, he does not attain fame; if he desires fame, he does not attain pleasure. Without reflection, one finds no resolution anywhere. 12.10.19 One must not cause injury to another’s mind; one must never be negligent. For one who is patient by nature, there is no loss of standing. 12.10.20
Whether for oneself or for another, every task must be performed; it is not ordained that a duty should be abandoned on account of circumstances.

(21) It is known through direct experience that one’s own happiness arises from pleasant words; therefore, one should consider others as one considers oneself. (22) It is an experienced fact that pain arises from harsh words; so why, then, should one speak harshly? (23)
When there is a vicegerent upon one's own body, then the living soul becomes distressed. By this experience of one's own, one ought to protect others.
(24) That which causes suffering to another is impure speech (*vaikharī*). At some time or on some occasion, it will bring about our own destruction.
(25) As we sow, so shall we reap; as we speak, so shall the answer come. Then why must one speak harshly? (26)
One should bring happiness to many people through the greatness of one's own human purpose; however, to produce suffering is the demonic way (rākṣasī kriyā). 27.
It is stated in the Bhagavad Gītā that hypocrisy, pride, conceit, anger, and harsh speech are the characteristics of ignorance. 28.
He who is adorned with the highest qualities is indeed a great and virtuous person (satpuruṣa); many people wander about seeking him. 29.

Knowledge of words without action is like a dog vomiting; the virtuous never behold such a thing. (30) People seek out those great souls who practice devotion with their minds and diligently maintain excellent qualities. (31) Thus, he who is a person of noble character should form a community; through the yoga of devotion, the God of gods should be made one's own. (32) 12.10.32

If one's own death should occur unexpectedly, by whom should worship be performed? Therefore, an arrangement must be made for the worship of many people. 12.10.33 Our vow is this: nothing at all should be requested from the disciple. After oneself, the disciple should simply offer devotion to the Lord of the World (this alone is to be prayed for). 12.10.34 Therefore, let there be a community; let there be a great festival. Let effort be made so that God may be attained with little exertion. 35
Now, two characteristics are necessary for the collective purpose so that listeners may give their attention to this subject.
(12.10.36) That means by which many people practice devotion is called the power of awakening (*prabodhana-śakti*). For that purpose, it is necessary to know the minds of many.

(12.10.37) People regard as an authority that person in whom the excellent qualities previously mentioned reside. A description of the characteristics of the power of awakening will follow later. (12.10.38)

People consider the word of one who acts according to what he says to be authoritative; people consider the word of one who first acts and subsequently speaks to be authoritative. (12.10.39) That which is not approved by people, people do not accept. One is alone in the world, whereas people are many. (12.10.40) Therefore, [the teacher] should be with the people. Honoring and respecting the people, he should teach them. Through discernment, he should gradually lead them to the ultimate goal through discernment. (41)
This is the supreme task of discrimination; a person endowed with discrimination will perform this by rule. Other wretched people, through delusion, engage only in quarreling.

(42) Quarreling with many will occur even for a single person without an army; therefore, many people must be made content. 12.10.43 Abandon all misfortune. One should maintain excellent characteristics such as listening to the stories of Hari, listening to the Purāṇas, ethics, logic, and so forth. 13.10.22

Discernment in conduct consists precisely in this: that all people may become well-disposed. Their merit must be cultivated gradually. (To teach a child,) one must proceed with the pace of a child; one must speak with the manner of a child. In the same way, people are to be awakened very slowly. October 13, 24. The primary task is indeed the protection of the inner thoughts of people; this alone is the mark of wisdom. He who is wise knows the fourfold limb [of action] (he knows the task in its entirety); others, however, are fools. October 13, 25.

Even so, a fool should not be driven away by the word "fool. One should never expose the vital weakness of anyone through speech. Acting in this manner, one who is free from desire accomplishes the conquest of the quarters.

(13.10.26) Various situations arise in various places; having understood them, one should carry out the task in its entirety. (Being free from desire,) one should become the inner self of every living being. (13.10.27)
Having preserved what is in the mind, one should depart; for there remains a longing to meet again. If one departs having broken the heart’s intent (being devoid of desire), disorder arises.
13.10.28 Therefore, he who preserves what is in the mind is a great saint. If the heart’s intent is preserved, all people are attracted.
13.10.29 In the Kali age, *kīrtana* should be performed. Only that which is soft and skillful should be sung; the harsh, the rough, and the distorted must be abandoned on one side. 14.1.1
For that indeed is poetry which, like a garland fashioned from the flowers of well-chosen words— filled with the intense fragrance of extraordinary meaning—
satisfies the swarm of bees that are the virtuous through its abundance of scent. This very garland,
strung together within my heart, is now to be offered at the feet of the Hero of the Raghus.
Nevertheless, the thread of the *praṇava*, following the inner core of the garland, must not be severed.
(2) If there is such poetic skill, let it be employed at will for the benefit of others.
Now, however, I shall demonstrate it for the sake of illustration; listen to the characteristics of good poetry. (3)
One should strive by the hundreds of means to acquire such poetic skill that devotion may arise for the lotus feet of the Lord and that the state of detachment may increase;
for that knowledge which is mere verbalism and devoid of practice is not highly esteemed by the wise.
Therefore, through remorse, one should first cultivate serenity toward the Lord.
(5) Now, whatever word proceeds from the mouth of the Supreme Lord after his favor has been won—that shall be known as worthy of praise; they declare that to be *prāsādika* poetry. (6)
They say that poetry is of three kinds: the bold (*dhṛṣṭa*), the recited (*paṭhita*), and the pleasing (*prāsādika*).
Therefore, since these three types of poetry are well-known, their mutual distinction is now defined:
[7] That which is composed with boldness is the "bold" (*dhṛṣṭa*); it is that which expresses what is in the mind or is uttered as such.
They declare that poetry in which words are dragged out by force and the like is known as *dhṛṣṭa* (bold).
If what is situated in the throat is recited with great rattling, that is called *paṭhita* (recited);
or if various imitations are made after looking into other texts, that too is called *paṭhita*. ||8-9||
That poetry which is hastily composed, which merely follows what is seen,
and likewise that which is fashioned devoid of devotion— they declare such poetry to be "bold recitation" (dhṛṣṭapāṭha).
[But that which] awakens desire, is adorned with aesthetic flavor (rasa), or possesses the erotic, heroic, and comic sentiments—
They declare that poetry is a diversion filled with curiosity and sorrow, characterized by bold expression (dhṛṣṭapāṭha).

When one’s mental state is overwhelmed by desire, then such a sound issues from the mouth; however, this occurs through poetry—that is, through bold expression—and yet no one reaches the further shore of the ocean of existence. 11–12.
A hymn to Agni, who resides within the stomach for the sake of providing nourishment, should also be sung here by men.

That which displays ingenuity in this regard is declared to be *dhṛṣṭapāṭha* (bold recitation), and that is poetry (*kāvyam*). Poetry would not exist at all as *dhṛṣṭapāṭha* if it were merely a composition of words forcibly dragged together.
Poetry should never be possessed of arrogance; poetry should not be designated by heretical doctrines.
Poetry should never be full of dispute; poetry should not cause the disruption of aesthetic flavor (rasa).
Poetry should never be a failure of stage-effect; poetry should not be devoid of illustrative examples.
Poetry should be florid yet not excessively so; it should not fail to convey its intended subject.
That is not poetry which, upon observing crooked men, adopts a similarly crooked manner.
Poetry should never be inferior, nor should there be the fault of redundancy in it.
Let there be no violation of the meter, nor should it be devoid of its own name-seal (svanāmamudrā).

Poetry that lacks etymological derivation, or is unphilosophical, lacking in artistic skill, or bereft of beautiful words—nor indeed poetry that is deficient in knowledge, devotion, or renunciation—shall never come to be. (17–18)
