One should consider that poetry which is devoid of devotion to be foolish;
indeed, speech lacking love will certainly cause distress where it is intended as poetry.
Furthermore, a mere restatement made without devotion should be understood as nothing more than a trivial amusement.
If there is love for the Supreme Lord, how could there not be poetry that brings Him into harmony with one’s heart?
(20) Let it be so; indeed, this bold recitation here is merely a delusion arising from vain pride.
Now, another kind of poetry, which was previously described as "gracious" (*prāsādika*), is being examined. (21)
Whatever wealth, pleasure, or gold one may possess, it is all equal to vomit.
Likewise, even while remaining within the inner self, his meditation is always upon the One who is supreme in all qualities;
at every moment, his supreme joy resides in the lotus feet of the Blessed Lord;
and at every moment, his supreme delight increases in the worship of Hari.
He who does not spend even a single moment in vain, devoid of devotion to the Divine,
but remains at all times inwardly truly colored by devotion—
within whose inner self the Lord Himself resides, established with ease and immovably. (24)

Whatever has been spoken by him [the Lord] by his very nature is the definitive description of the reality of Brahman. (26) The Lord is inwardly established within him, and through that, a delight in devotion arises.
Such is this state that, once one is separated from devotion, no other discourse issues from his mouth. (26)
When devotion flashes within the inner self, then the manifest speech (vaikharī) likewise proceeds;
and he who, full of emotion and drenched in compassion, chants with love while dancing—
by whom the inner self is fixed on the Lord and the perception of the body is no longer remembered.

Fear and shame—these two flee far away when one is at a distance from the feet [of the Lord]. (28) He who is colored by the hue of love and who is intoxicated by the pride of devotion—such a person, thinking "I am the best of devotees," has this very state cast beneath the feet. (29)
How indeed can he behold this world while singing and dancing with such fearlessness,
since the Lord of the Three Worlds has arrived and taken his seat within his pair of eyes? He who is thus supremely devoted to the Lord need not seek any other object of value.
He describes at his own will the meditation, the fame, and likewise the majesty of the Lord.
Various meditations and many forms, various majesties and much fame—
all this praise before that Man, I consider to be truly equal to a blade of grass.

Let it be so: he who wanders through this phenomenal world detached, being such a devotee of the Lord, is indeed the highest of devotees; he is liberated and is approved by the assembly of the virtuous.
His playfulness in speech is truly his devotion, and that is known as poetry characterized by clarity.
Whatever speech he utters with ease, therein discernment shall be revealed.
(34) Therefore, listen to the excellent characteristics of poetry, which were previously declared and are now stated again;
by this description of its characteristics, the inner heart of the audience is pleased. (35)
Indeed, that poetry may become exceedingly pure; likewise, that poetry may become simple.
Indeed, that poetry may be of such a kind that its lineage is filled with simplicity.
(36) Truly, poetry may arise from the yoga of devotion; indeed, poetry may possess extraordinary meaning.
This kind of poetic skill would indeed arise from that which has emerged far removed from egoism (37).
Poetic skill would be filled with the glory of Hari; poetic skill would be sweet and beautiful;
poetic skill would be the majesty of the Blessed One, wherein there exists a style completely full of vital energy (38).
May there be poetry endowed with easily understood meaning; may there be poetry possessed of a beautiful form.
May there likewise be poetry that is easy to recite, and may there be poetry composed in [proper] meters.
May there be poetry that is soft, charming, auspicious, as well as tender and wonderful.
It should be endowed with sweetness, beautiful, extensive, and likewise filled with the sentiment of devotion (bhakti-rasa).
There should be various compositions of words and syllables characterized by skill;
much that is bound in meter with dexterity, as well as *dhāṭī* and *mudrā* in many ways. ||40-41||
May there be various methods, diverse intellects, manifold arts, and likewise various accomplishments;
may the means for those of diverse lineages and poetry likewise be of many kinds.
May there be various examples from literature, diverse logics, and invented narratives.
It contains various kinds of consensus, reasoned speech, and established doctrines along with their opposing arguments (pūrvapakṣa);

it possesses diverse derivations and understandings, as well as manifold insights and inspirations; and whether it has various forms of resolve or retention—wherever these exist, that is the poetry praised here. (43–44)
Doubts, counter-questions, and their answers are presented as poetic verses in accordance with the principles of the scriptures;
by reflecting deeply upon these, there will certainly be the removal of doubt.
There are various contexts, manifold deliberations, yoga, and likewise its various explanations.
That poem in which there is the essence of various kinds of inquiry into reality is praised here.
(46) That poem in which there are various means of pilgrimage, wandering to sacred fords, diverse austerities, and the dispelling of manifold doubts is praised here. (47)
That by which remorse arises and conformity to worldly opinion is disregarded, and likewise that by which knowledge is born within—the heart—only such is praised here as true poetry.
Furthermore, that by which the power of knowledge increases and by which one’s worldly livelihood may be set aside [is also so praised]. (48)
That by which the path of devotion is realized is alone the excellent true poetry praised here;

(49) that by which the notion of the body is shattered, by which this ocean of worldly existence becomes dried up, and by which the direct perception of the Lord is attained—that alone is the excellent true poetry praised here. (50)
That alone is praised here as true poetry by which right understanding may sprout, by which the refutation of heresy may occur,
by which discernment may be awakened,
by which the perception of reality may arise, and by which this delusion may be dispelled. (51)
That which is devoid of these defects shall be recognized here as true poetry, and that alone is praised.
(52) That by which the mind attains composure, by which the bondage of saṃsāra is severed, and which the virtuous also hold in high esteem—that alone is true poetry, and it is praised here. (53)
If the characteristics pertaining to excellent poetry were to be described in this manner, they would indeed become excessively prolix.
Therefore, I have here set forth merely a few illustrations for the sole purpose of further delighting the listeners.
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Description of the Art of Poetry," in the *Śrī Dāsabodha*, a dialogue between teacher and disciple.

There are various modes of dress and various stages of life (*āśramas*), yet the root of them all is the householder’s stage (*gṛhasthāśrama*). Here, the inhabitants of the three worlds find their rest. 14.7.1 Gods, sages, ascetics, various forest-dwellers, those free from passion, guests, visitors, and ancestors—all these are sharers in the householder’s state.

14.7.2 Though they were born in the householder’s stage, they have departed from it to become renunciants; nevertheless, it is only the houses of householders that they wander through, bearing their fame. 14.7.3

Therefore, among all stages of life (*āśramas*), the householder’s stage (*gṛhasthāśrama*) is the best. Nevertheless, it is essential that therein one’s own duty (*svadharma*) and compassion for all beings (*bhūtadayā*) be present. 14.7.4 That [householder’s stage] is the best wherein the six duties (*ṣaṭ-karmāṇi*) are performed, ritual actions are carried out according to rule, and one speaks with sweet words toward every living creature. 14.7.5 The regular performance of actions prescribed by the scriptures is in every way excellent; even within that, there exists this extraordinary path of devotion (*bhaktimārga*). 14.7.6

Performing preparatory rites (*puraścaraṇa*), emaciating his body, firm in his vows, and enduring extreme hardship, he—being a householder yet transcending the worldly—considered nothing other than the Lord of the Universe.

With his body, speech, mind, and vital breaths, he bore all suffering for the sake of the Blessed One. A firm resolve regarding the path of devotion was formed within his mind. Such is the devotee of the Blessed One, who is especially detached within his inner self; having abandoned worldly existence for the sake of the Divine, he becomes liberated.

That which is dispassion within the inner organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is itself to be understood as great fortune; there is no misfortune comparable to greed. 14.7.10 Be it so; that circumstance which has thus occurred is now past. Now, however, let the Brahmins be clever.
14.8.1 (By the Brahmins) the Lord is to be worshipped with pure hands; by that, all become fortunate. Those who are fools, lacking devotion, and undisciplined—they experience poverty. 14.8.2
First, the Divine is to be known; thereafter, He is to be worshipped with undivided devotion. One should perform uninterrupted meditation upon the Supreme of all.

(14.8.3) He who is the best among all is called the "Supreme of All" (*sarvottama*). Through meditation upon Him, the essential point of the discrimination between the Self and the non-Self must be understood. (14.8.4) The Self protects the body through knowledge; it is the seer and the inner witness. Through knowledge, it examines all objects. (14.8.5)

It is one's own direct experience that He dwells within the bodies of all living beings and impels the aggregate of the senses. 14.8.6 He who dwells in all living beings dwells within the universe; therefore, the inner organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) must be cultivated. He alone is the giver to one another, and He alone is the enjoyer for one another. Whatever exists, He alone is that. 14.8.7 It should be rightly perceived that the Divine dwells within the universe, He alone dwells within our inner self, and He alone dwells in every living being throughout the three worlds. 14.8.8

From the very beginning, the Seer is one; He is omnipresent. Due to the influence of the body and material nature, He appears as if divided and distinct. 14.8.9 Previously, the listeners asked about the characteristics of the topics concerning the narrations of Hari. Now, let the wise listen attentively to the answer. 14.5.1 To be a servant of Hari while being detached, to be a devotee full of love while being a knower, and to be free from argumentative speech while being highly learned—this is unprecedented. 14.5.4

Those who, while the qualified form (saguṇamūrti) exists before them, initiate discourse on the unqualified (nirguṇa) and proceed to negate the qualified, are fools among scholars. 14.5.10 It is a matter of direct perception that whatever line there is, it is subject to washing away; nevertheless, why is the eyes closed (as if to ignore the obvious)? 15.6.9 He who accepts the words of many is destroyed by mere inference; he possesses no primary certainty rooted in direct experience. 15.6.10

One must listen to the many words of many people, but they should be examined by means of reason. The determination of their truth or falsehood must be held within one's own heart. 15.6.11 One should not say "no" to anyone. Both pitfalls and means must be understood; one should simply accept what is credible. What is the use of further talk? 15.6.12 Even for a speck of dust there are minute insects, whose lifespan is exceedingly short; their logic and intellect are likewise measured by that same standard. 15.8.1

Thus, there exist various living beings (*jīva*s). Although they do not come within the range of perception, nevertheless, the fivefold internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) exists even within them. (15.8.2) For their sake, [the world] is sufficient; their knowledge, as well as objects and sense organs, is the same. Who indeed could perceive such subtle bodies? (15.8.3) That insect considers even an ant to be large; thus it is said, "An elephant has passed by. Even for an ant, the stream of human urine is like a flood—such is the popular saying. (15.8.4)
From the fruits, the flowers are older; from the flowers, the leaves are older; from the leaves, the entire pieces of wood are older.
From the wood, the fine roots are older; from the roots, water is the oldest. When that water becomes dry, it becomes the terrestrial world.
Thus he gains this conviction: therefore, the earth is older than all those [elements]; and even older than the earth is the form of Nārāyaṇa in the form of water.

Therefore, Agni-deva is the eldest; Vāyu-deva is the eldest of Agni; and the true form of the Inner Self is the eldest of Vāsudeva. (15.9.17) The Inner Self is the eldest of all; he who does not know Him is a wicked soul (*durātmā*). A "wicked soul" is one by whom the Self has been cast far away.
(15.9.18) One should go wherever the story of Hari is told; there, one should sit like a wretched person at a distance, and hold in one's heart every essential point concerning Him. (19.2.20)
Therein, the highest persons are found; those who are all-pervading are also known. (By their path) one should proceed forward very slowly, step by step.

19.2.2 Therefore, having made the internal organ attentive, listen to the characteristics of the unfortunate. Following the abandonment of these characteristics, the characteristics of the fortunate arise.
19.3.1 The unfortunate person, due to sin, attains poverty; from poverty, he accumulates sin. In this very manner, it proceeds moment by moment. 19.3.2

Some intense quality is necessary; know that without it, fame will never arise. What is accomplished by wandering aimlessly about? 19.6.24 There is no trust in the body. Who knows when life will come to an end, or what kind of circumstance will befall us? 19.6.25
